game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 4, 10.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 4, 9.
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is 12.5, the sum of the expected values of the three dice:
- Die 1: 15/4 = 3.75
- Die 2: 20/8 = 2.5
- Die 3: 50/8 = 6.25

The settlement value is very uncertain at this point. Its variance is about 33.6 (standard deviation about 5.8). Half of counterparties know the exact value, so a tight quote would mostly get picked off by them. I am quoting 4 either side of fair value.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 16.5}

The prior expected value of the sum is 12.5: die 1 averages 3.75, die 2 averages 2.5 and die 3 averages 6.25.

At quote 1 someone sold to me at 8.5, below that prior. An informed trader only does that when the true value is under 8.5, so this is evidence the value is lower than 12.5. I'm shading my estimate of fair value down to about 11.

I'm already long 1, so I'll skew both prices down to lean toward selling. I'll keep the spread wide because half the counterparties are informed.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 14.5}

The prior expected sum is 3.75 + 2.5 + 6.25 = 12.5.

The two trades so far roughly cancel out. A counterparty sold at 8.5, which hints the value is low. Another bought at 14.5, which hints it is high. So my estimate stays near 12.5.

I'll quote a fairly wide spread around that value. The settlement is very uncertain, and half of counterparties know it exactly, so a wide spread protects against them.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 16.0}

The posterior on the settlement value is split between low outcomes and 17–18, with an expected value of about 10.2. Because the uncertainty is wide, I'm posting a wide quote centred near that value.

**Prior after the reveal.** Die 1 = 0, so the contract settles at die 2 + die 3. Die 2 averages 2.5 and die 3 averages 6.25, giving an expected value of 8.75. The range is 0 to 18.

**What the trades suggest.**
- Buys at 14.5 and 16 are hard to explain by an informed trader now that die 1 = 0. A total above 14.5 needs die 2 = 9 and die 3 of 7, 8 or 9, giving totals of 16, 17 or 18. That has a prior probability of about 9%.
- The buy at 16 is stronger evidence still, since only totals of 17 or 18 clear it.
- Noise traders could also explain those buys, each with roughly a 25–30% chance. The sell at 8.5 points the other way, towards a low total.

**Posterior.** Weighting each outcome by the prior and by the chance of seeing this trade history, about 36% of the probability sits on 17–18. Most of the rest sits on totals below 8.5. That gives the expected value of about 10.2.

**Quote.** I'm centred slightly above that, at 6.5 / 14.0, which leans a little towards buying back my short position of 1.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 14.0}

Die 1 = 0. Die 2 mean = 20/8 = 2.5. Die 3 mean = 50/8 = 6.25. Prior mean is 8.75 (sum of these two).

What happened in stage 1:
- Quotes 2 and 3 were buys well above 14, which points to a high die 1, but die 1 turned out to be 0. Those trades now look like noise.
- Quote 4 (bid 6.5, ask 14) brought no trade. That suggests the value sits somewhere between 6.5 and 14 or so.

Die 3 is likely 7–9 (6 of 8 faces). Possible sums of the two hidden dice:
- With die 3 at 7–9 and die 2 typically 0–4, the sum is roughly 7–13.
- With die 3 at 0 or 2, the sum is low.

The no-trade at quote 4 rules out low values somewhat, so fair value is about 9.

I'll quote a bid of 7 and an ask of 12.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 12}

Die 1 = 0, so the settlement value is die 2 + die 3. With die 1 known, the expected value from the dice alone is 2.5 + 6.25 = 8.75.

**Update from quote 5.** Someone bought at 12, which pushes my estimate up.
- An informed buyer would need die 2 + die 3 above 12. That happens with probability 10/64 ≈ 0.16, and the average sum in those cases is about 15.4.
- A noise trader would need noise above roughly 3.25, which happens about 29% of the time.
- Weighting the two cases, there is roughly a 35% chance the value is in the high group. That puts fair value at about 10.3.

**Quote.** I am short 2, so I set my quotes slightly above that 10.3 estimate. The spread is wide to protect against the large spread of possible values.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13}

Die 1 = 0 and die 3 = 9, so settlement = 9 + die 2. Die 2 is one of {0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 4, 9}, so settlement is one of {9, 9, 9, 10, 11, 13, 13, 18}.

The prior mean is 9 + 2.5 = 11.5. In stage 2, counterparties bought at my asks of 12 and 13. Some of those buyers may have been informed, which points to a higher die 2. I estimate fair value at about 12 to 12.5.

I am short 3 and only one more sale is allowed before my ask is pulled at -4, so I want to lean toward buying back.
- **Bid 10.5:** an informed counterparty sells to me only when the value is 9 or 10. Noise traders around fair value will also hit it fairly often, which reduces my short.
- **Ask 14.5:** an informed counterparty buys only when the value is 18.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 14.5}

The contract settles at 9 + die 2 (die 1 = 0, die 3 = 9). On its own, die 2 averages 2.5, which would put fair value at 11.5. But the buy at 14.5 on quote 7 points towards die 2 = 9:

- If die 2 = 9 (value 18), a buy at 14.5 happens with probability about 0.65.
- For any other face, it happens with probability about 0.15.
- Updating on that, P(die 2 = 9) ≈ 0.38.
- That gives a fair value of about 13.4.

I'm short 4, so only the bid is open. An informed seller hits the bid only if the true value is below it, which means a value of 9, 10 or 11. Noise sellers hit it when 13.4 plus their noise falls below the bid. Expected profit per quote by bid level:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 11.5 | ≈ 0 |
| 10.5 | ≈ 0.23 |
| 10 | ≈ 0.35 |
| 9.5 | ≈ 0.42 |

A bid of 9.5 gives the best expected profit.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": null}

The contract now settles at 9 + die 2, since die 1 is 0 and die 3 is 9.

**Fair value.** Die 2 averages 20/8 = 2.5, so the settlement value V has a mean of 11.5. The eight equally likely outcomes are 9, 9, 9, 10, 11, 13, 13 and 18. No trade at quote 8 tells us little, so I take the fair value as about 11.5.

**Effect of the bid level.** At any bid of 9 or below, an informed seller never trades, because V is never below 9. The only counterparty who sells to me is a noise trader whose valuation falls below my bid. Each such trade earns about 11.5 minus the bid. Expected profit is 0.5 × P(noise valuation < bid) × (11.5 − bid):

| Bid | P(noise trader sells) | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| 9.0 | 0.333 | 0.42 |
| 8.5 | 0.302 | 0.45 |
| 8.0 | 0.273 | 0.48 |
| 7.5 | 0.245 | 0.49 |
| 7.0 | 0.219 | 0.49 |

Above 9, informed sellers start trading when V = 9 and the expected profit falls (about 0.27 at 9.5 and 0.11 at 10). The best region is about 7.0 to 7.5, so I bid 7.3. The ask stays null because my position is −4.

{"bid": 7.3, "ask": null}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The contract settles at the sum of three dice, so before any reveal its expected value is 10.5, with a standard deviation of about 2.96.

I compared half-spreads of 2 and 3 around 10.5. For each, I weighed the expected gain from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders. Figures below are per side of the quote.

- **Half-spread of 3 (quote 7.5 / 13.5):**
  - Noise traders: with noise standard deviation 4.4, a noise trader crosses one side with probability about 0.248. That gives about 0.65 × 0.248 × 3 ≈ 0.48 expected gain.
  - Informed traders: they only trade when the sum is 14 or more. Their average edge past 13.5 is about 0.243, so the expected loss is about 0.35 × 0.243 ≈ 0.085.
  - Net is about +0.40.
- **Half-spread of 2 (quote 8.5 / 12.5):**
  - Noise traders: crossing probability rises to about 0.325, but each trade earns less: 0.65 × 0.325 × 2 ≈ 0.42.
  - Informed traders: they trade on sums of 13 or more, with average edge about 0.454, so the expected loss is about 0.35 × 0.454 ≈ 0.159.
  - Net is about +0.26.

The wider quote does better, so I quote 7.5 bid and 13.5 ask.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

A noise trader selling at 7.5 is fairly likely, so the sale only moves my estimate of the value down moderately.

**Updated estimate after the sale at 7.5**
- Before any trades, the expected sum is 10.5.
- If the seller was informed (probability 0.35), the sum must be 7 or less.
  - That happens with probability 35/216 ≈ 0.16.
  - The average sum in that case is 6.0.
- If the seller was a noise trader (probability 0.65), it sold because its valuation was below 7.5.
  - That happens with probability about 0.25.
  - The sale tells me nothing about the dice, so the expected sum stays 10.5.
- Weighting the two cases, the chance the seller was informed is about 26%.
- The updated expected sum is therefore about 9.3.

**Quote**
- I am long 1 unit, so I shift both prices slightly down to make another sale to me less likely and a purchase from me more likely.
- I keep the spread wide because an informed trader still has a large edge over me.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 12.0}

Die 1 shows 5, and dice 2 and 3 each average 3.5, so fair value is 5 + 3.5 + 3.5 = 12.

The two stage-1 trades (one sell at 7.5, one buy at 12) point in opposite directions, so they roughly cancel and don't move fair value.

The two unrevealed dice have a standard deviation of about 2.4 combined. Noise traders are wider, with a standard deviation of 4.4. A spread of about ±2 around 12 is enough to cover losses to informed traders while still trading with most noise traders.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 14}

Die 1 (5) and die 2 (4) are known, so the sum is 9 plus die 3. The settlement value is therefore between 10 and 15, and the fair value is 9 + 3.5 = 12.5.

**Ask side.** I compared the expected profit per quote at several ask prices. Each figure is noise-trader profit minus expected loss to informed traders.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 13.1 | about 0.01 |
| 14.1 | about 0.32 |
| 15.1 | about 0.47 |
| 15.9 | about 0.48 |
| 16.5 | about 0.47 |

- At 15.1 and above, an informed trader never buys, because the value cannot exceed 15.
- Profit is flat around 15.9, so I set the ask at 15.9.

**Bid side.** The problem is symmetric around 12.5, so I set the bid at 12.5 − 3.4 = 9.1.

**Position limits.** My position is 0, so a single trade cannot breach the ±3 limit.

{"bid": 9.1, "ask": 15.9}

With die 1 = 5 and die 2 = 4 revealed, the known part is 9. Die 3 adds 1 to 6, so settlement is somewhere from 10 to 15. Fair value is 12.5, and the trade history doesn't change that.

**Choosing the ask:**
- An informed trader only buys if the true value is above my ask. Any ask above 15 can never be hit by an informed trader.
- Noise traders value the contract at 12.5 plus noise with standard deviation 4.4. My expected noise profit is 0.65 × P(noise > ask − 12.5) × (ask − 12.5).
- At an ask of 15.1, this gives about 0.47.
- At an ask of 16.0, it gives about 0.485, the best of the levels I checked.
- At an ask of 16.5, it falls back to about 0.47.

So an ask of about 16.0 is best.

**Choosing the bid:** the payoffs are symmetric around 12.5, so the bid mirrors the ask at about 9.0. That is below 10, so an informed trader will never sell to me.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 16.0}

A spread of 2 on each side balances these. That gives a bid of 8.5 and an ask of 12.5.

A half-spread of about 1.5 should earn from noise traders while limiting losses to informed ones, so I'll quote 9.0 / 12.0.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 12.0}

Fair value before any trades was 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. Someone selling to me at 9 is weak evidence that the sum is low, so I estimate fair value at about 10.3. I'm long 1 unit, so I'm shading both sides slightly lower to make it easier to sell back.

{"bid": 8.7, "ask": 11.7}

With die 1 = 6 and two dice still unknown, the fair value is 6 + 3.5 + 3.5 = 13. The remaining uncertainty from the two hidden dice is about ±2.4, so I keep a fairly wide spread for protection against informed traders. Last quote's spread of ±1.5 got no trade, so I tighten it slightly to ±1.2 around 13.

{"bid": 11.8, "ask": 14.2}

Die 1 = 6, so the fair value is 6 + 3.5 + 3.5 = 13, with a range of 8 to 18. The buy at 14.2 hints slightly at a higher value, so I shade the fair value up a little to about 13.2. I'm short 1, so I lean the quote slightly higher too.

{"bid": 11.8, "ask": 14.6}

Die 1 = 6 and die 2 = 2 give 8. Die 3 averages 3.5, so fair value is **11.5**, and settlement can only be 9 to 14.

I compared expected profit per side for different spreads:
- **Noise traders (80%)** are the profit source. A wider spread earns more per trade, but fewer of them trade.
- **Informed traders (20%)** only cost me when the true value is beyond my quote.

At ±2.4 from fair (bid 9.1, ask 13.9):
- An informed buyer only trades if die 3 is 6 (value 14), losing me just 0.1.
- An informed seller only trades if die 3 is 1 (value 9), also losing 0.1.
- Noise traders still trade about 21% of the time on each side, earning 2.4 each.

That works out to roughly 0.4 expected profit per side. This beats tighter quotes: about 0.34 at 10/13 and about 0.26 at 10.4/12.6.

My short position of -1 is small, so I keep the quote symmetric around fair.

{"bid": 9.1, "ask": 13.9}

Public fair value is about 11.9. Die 1 + die 2 = 8, and die 3 is still unknown (1–6), so the sum settles between 9 and 14.

- **Starting point:** before quote 7 the fair value was 11.5.
- **What quote 7 tells us:** someone bought at 13.9. An informed trader would only do that if the value is 14, meaning die 3 = 6. A noise trader buys there with probability about 0.21.
- **Updated odds:** using Bayes' rule, the chance the value is 14 rises to about 0.305. Each of 9–13 falls to about 0.139.
- **Result:** the expected value is 0.139 × (9+10+11+12+13) + 0.305 × 14, which is about 11.9.

I'm short 2, so I set the quotes around 11.9 to limit losses to an informed trader:
- **Bid 10.4:** an informed seller only hits it if the value is 9 or 10.
- **Ask 13.4:** an informed buyer only lifts it if the value is 14.

{"bid": 10.4, "ask": 13.4}

- The first term is what I earn from noise traders who cross my quote.
- The second term is what informed traders take from me.
- In this formula, P(Z > x) is the standard normal upper-tail probability and φ is the standard normal density.

| h | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 6.4 | about 0.48 |
| 8 | about 0.52 |
| 9 | about 0.47 |

The fair value is about 13.9, so I'll quote a wide market around it: bid 10, ask 18.

**Fair value.** The deck has 11 cards worth 51 in total, so the average card is 51/11 ≈ 4.64. Three cards give an expected sum of about 13.9.

**How the outcome is spread.** The sum depends mostly on how many 11s are dealt:

| Number of 11s dealt | Probability | Approximate sum |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 34% | 6–9 |
| 1 | 51% | 15–17 |
| 2 | 15% | about 24 |

**Checking the bid at 10.**
- Informed traders sell to me when the value is below 10. That happens about 34% of the time, and I lose about 2 per trade.
- Noise traders sell to me about 26% of the time, and I gain about 3.9 per trade.
- Expected profit on the bid is about 0.65 × 0.26 × 3.9 − 0.35 × 0.34 × 2 ≈ +0.42.

**Checking the ask at 18.**
- Informed traders buy from me when the value is above 18. That happens about 15% of the time, and I lose about 6.5 per trade.
- Noise traders buy from me about 26% of the time, and I gain about 4.1 per trade.
- Expected profit on the ask is about 0.65 × 0.26 × 4.1 − 0.35 × 0.15 × 6.5 ≈ +0.35.

Both sides have positive expected profit.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 18}

Using the card mix, the expected sum is about 13.9. The seller at 10 makes a low hand, with no 11s, more likely. That pushes fair value down to about 11. I'm quoting wide around it because informed traders are common.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 14.5}

Card 1 = 3. Remaining 10 cards: 0, 2,2,2, 3,3,3, 11,11,11, so each remaining card has mean 45/10 = 4.5 and the two unrevealed cards sum to an expected 9. That puts fair value at 3 + 9 = 12.

The trade history gives mixed signals: one counterparty sold at 10 and one bought at 14.5, roughly cancelling out. I keep fair value near 12.

The sum of the two remaining cards can only take a few values:
- Two small cards (from 0, 2, 3) give 0 to 6, so the total lands around 5 to 9.
- One 11 plus a small card gives about 16 to 17.
- Two 11s give 25.

So the payoff is very spread out. Informed traders will trade on whichever side their value falls, and noise traders have a standard deviation of 6.2. A spread of about 4.5 around 12 seems reasonable.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 14.5}

Card 1 is 3, so 10 cards remain: one 0, three 2s, three 3s and three 11s. Their average is 4.8, so two more cards add 9.6 on average. That puts the public fair value at about 12.6.

The last trade was a buy at 14.5. For an informed trader to buy there, the settlement must be above 14.5. That means the two hidden cards include at least one 11, which has a probability of about 53%. A noise trader would buy at 14.5 only about 38% of the time. So that buy nudges my estimate up to roughly 13.5.

I am short 1, so I quote a wide spread with a slight upward lean, centred near 13.5.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 16.5}

With cards 1 and 2 both 3, the revealed sum is 6, and 9 cards remain.

**Remaining deck**
- One 0
- Three 2s
- Two 3s
- Three 11s

**Possible settlements**

| Settlement | Third card | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 0 | 1/9 |
| 8 | 2 | 3/9 |
| 9 | 3 | 2/9 |
| 17 | 11 | 3/9 |

The expected settlement value is about 11. Noise traders value the contract at 11 plus noise with standard deviation 6.2.

**Bid:** At 7.5, an informed trader only sells when the settlement is 6. That loses 1.5 with probability 1/9, so the expected cost is about 0.06. Noise traders sell below 7.5 about 29% of the time, earning 3.5 each time, which is worth about 0.66. A lower bid adds almost nothing, and a bid at 8 or higher starts selling to informed traders when the settlement is 8.

**Ask:** At 16.5, an informed trader buys when the settlement is 17. That loses 0.5 with probability 1/3, so the expected cost is about 0.06. Noise traders buy above 16.5 about 19% of the time, earning 5.5 each time, which is worth about 0.67. Asks around 14 do much worse because every informed buy at 17 then costs about 3. I'm short 1, so selling one more unit stays within the position limit.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 16.5}

Card 3 is drawn from the 9 cards left: one 0, three 2s, two 3s and three 11s. With 6 already showing, the settlement value is:

| Settlement | 6 | 8 | 9 | 17 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/9 | 3/9 | 2/9 | 3/9 |

That gives a fair value of 99/9 = 11. This is the last quote, so I only need the expected profit of one trade on each side.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only if the value is above my ask, which here means only when it is 17.
- At an ask of 17 the informed trader never buys, because 17 is not above 17.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(Normal noise > 6) ≈ 0.166.
- Expected profit is 0.65 × 0.166 × 6 ≈ +0.65.
- For comparison, an ask of 16 gives about +0.57, 15 about +0.44 and 18 about +0.59. So 17 is best.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only if the value is below my bid.
- At a bid of 6 the informed trader never sells, because 6 is not below 6.
- A noise trader sells with probability P(Normal noise < -5) ≈ 0.21.
- Expected profit is 0.65 × 0.21 × 5 ≈ +0.68.
- For comparison, a bid of 7 gives about +0.63 and 8.9 about +0.39. So 6 is best.

Either fill keeps my position within the ±3 limit.

game.title: Dice/cards count
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12.
- Die 2 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/10), 4 (prob 1/5), 5 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 1/10), 8 (prob 3/10), 9 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dice showing at least 7.

info.raw:
Fair value is 11.67. Die 1 shows at least 7 with probability 2/3 and die 2 with probability 1/2, so the contract settles at 0 (1/6), 10 (1/2) or 20 (1/3).

I set each side by trading off profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders.

- **Ask 19.5:** expected value is about +1.05 per quote. Noise traders buy with probability about 0.22 at roughly 7.8 above fair value. The only informed loss is when the contract settles at 20, which costs 0.5.
- **Bid 2.5:** expected value is about +0.9 to +0.95, nearly flat across bids of 2 to 3. Noise traders sell with probability about 0.18 at roughly 9.2 below fair value. The only informed loss is when the contract settles at 0, which costs 2.5.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 19.5}

Fair value now is about 11.2.

**Prior distribution.**
- Die 1 shows at least 7 with probability 4/6 = 2/3.
- Die 2 shows at least 7 with probability 1/2.
- So the settlement is 0 with probability 1/6, 10 with probability 1/2, and 20 with probability 1/3.
- The expected value is 10 × (2/3 + 1/2) = 11.67.

**Update from the no-trade on quote 1 (2.5 / 19.5).**
- An informed trader holding 0 would have sold at 2.5. An informed trader holding 20 would have bought at 19.5. So no trade rules out an informed counterparty when the value is 0 or 20.
- An informed trader at 10 never trades at those prices.
- A noise trader declines to trade about 60% of the time, roughly, at those prices.
- This shifts weight towards 10:
  - 0 has weight about 0.065.
  - 10 has weight about 0.37.
  - 20 has weight about 0.13.
- Normalised, the posterior mean is about 11.2.

**Quote.** I keep the quote fairly wide around 11.2 to protect against informed sellers when the value is 0 and informed buyers when it is 20. I tighten it slightly from quote 1 to pick up some noise-trader flow.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 18.0}

Die 2 = 9, so it counts as at least 7 and adds 10 for certain. Die 1 counts if it shows 7, 8, 10 or 12, which is 4 of 6 faces (probability 2/3). The contract therefore settles at either 10 or 20. Fair value is 10 + 10 × 2/3 ≈ 16.67.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only arrives when the value is 20, so any ask of 20 or more carries no informed risk. Noise buyers have valuations of about N(16.67, 10).

- Expected noise profit is 0.65 × (ask − 16.67) × P(valuation > ask).
- This peaks at about 1.10 for an ask between 24 and 25.
- I'll ask 24.5.

**Bid:** An informed seller only arrives when the value is 10, so any bid of 10 or less carries no informed risk.

- Expected noise profit is 0.65 × (16.67 − bid) × P(valuation < bid).
- This is about 1.09 at a bid of 10 and about 1.11 at 9, so it peaks around 9.
- I'll bid 9.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 24.5}

Die 2 is 9, which is at least 7, so it already contributes 10. Die 1 shows at least 7 on 4 of its 6 faces (7, 8, 10, 12). The contract therefore settles at 20 with probability 2/3 and at 10 with probability 1/3. Fair value is about 16.67. I'm treating the earlier no-trade quotes as carrying no useful information.

Expected profit from each side, using 0.65 for noise traders and 0.35 for informed traders:

- **Ask:**
  - Any ask at or below 20 gets hit by informed traders whenever the value is 20, which drags profit down.
  - An ask of 20 earns about 0.80.
  - Above 20, informed traders never buy, so only the noise-trader edge counts. That edge peaks at about 1.10 for asks between 24 and 25. I'll use 24.5.
- **Bid:**
  - Any bid at or below 10 is never hit by informed traders.
  - Bids from 8 to 10 each earn about 1.09.
  - A bid of 12 earns only about 0.74, because informed traders sell whenever the value is 10.
  - I'll use 9.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 24.5}

game.contract: The contract settles at the product of the two dice.

info.raw:
The public fair value moved from 12.25 to about 16 after the buy at 18.5, so I'm quoting wide around it with a slight upward lean.

**Prior.** The product of two dice has a mean of 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25.

**Which outcomes beat 18.5.** Eight of the 36 outcomes have a product above 18.5: 20, 20, 24, 24, 25, 30, 30 and 36. Their average is about 26.1. The other 28 outcomes average about 8.3.

**Chance of a buy at 18.5 in each case.**
- A noise trader buys if 12.25 plus noise exceeds 18.5. That happens with probability about 0.315.
- If the value is above 18.5, the informed trader always buys. So P(buy) = 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.315 ≈ 0.555.
- If the value is below 18.5, only noise traders buy. So P(buy) = 0.65 × 0.315 ≈ 0.205.

**Updated fair value.**
- High case weight: 0.222 × 0.555 ≈ 0.123.
- Low case weight: 0.778 × 0.205 ≈ 0.159.
- Updated mean: (0.123 × 26.1 + 0.159 × 8.3) / 0.282 ≈ 16.

**Quote.** I'm keeping the spread wide because informed traders make up 35% of counterparties. I'm leaning slightly upward because I'm short one unit and the evidence points higher.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 23}

The value is now die 2 alone, which is uniform on 1–6 with a fair value of 3.5. Informed traders can never value it above 6 or below 1. So any ask of at least 6 and any bid of at most 1 cannot be hit profitably by an informed trader.

That leaves the noise traders, whose valuations are 3.5 plus noise with standard deviation 13. For a spread x either side of 3.5, my expected profit per side is x times the chance they cross, P(Z > x/13). This is largest at roughly x ≈ 0.75 × 13 ≈ 9.8.

So I quote 3.5 ± 9.8: a bid of -6.3 and an ask of 13.3. This assumes negative prices are allowed. Being short 1 is well within the position limits, so both sides stay open.

{"bid": -6.3, "ask": 13.3}

**Ask:** Any ask of 6 or higher can never be lifted by an informed trader. So the only question is how far above 3.5 to sit against noise traders, whose valuations have a standard deviation of 13.
- Expected profit per quote is 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 3.5).
- At an ask of 10 this is about 1.30.
- At 15 it is about 1.40, which is the peak.
- At 17 it falls back to about 1.31.

**Bid:** Any bid of 1 or lower is safe from informed traders. The noise trade-off is symmetric around 3.5, so the best bid is about 3.5 − 11.5 = −8.

{"bid": -8, "ask": 15}

**Fair value**

| Settlement | Dice at 6 or more | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | neither | 0.1875 |
| 10 | one | 0.5 |
| 20 | both | 0.3125 |

On the ask side, an informed trader buys only when the settlement is 20. That happens with probability 0.2 × 0.3125 ≈ 0.06, and I lose 5 on it, so the expected loss is about 0.31. Noise traders lift the ask about 30% of the time, and each fill earns 3.75. That works out to roughly 0.89 of expected gain. The spread therefore clears adverse selection comfortably, and the bid side is roughly symmetric.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 15.0}

Prior fair value is 11.25. Die 1 shows at least 6 with probability 1/2, and die 2 with probability 5/8, so the value is 10 × (0.5 + 0.625).

Settlement takes only three values:

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 15.5}

**Ask side.** An informed buyer only lifts my ask if the value (10) is above it. So any ask above 10 carries no adverse selection.

- This is roughly 0.89 at 10, 0.95 at 11, 0.95 at 12 and similar at 11.5.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 11.5}

Die 1 shows 4, so only die 2 can count. Die 2 is at least 6 on 5 of its 8 faces, so the contract settles at 10 with probability 5/8 and at 0 otherwise. Fair value is 6.25.

**Last trade.** The buy at 11.5 tells us nothing. An informed trader knows the value is at most 10, so they would never buy at 11.5. The buyer must have been a noise trader, and fair value stays at 6.25.

- That peaks at about x = 0.75, which gives an ask of about 11.5.

**Bid.** At a bid of 0, an informed trader facing a value of 0 will not sell, because their valuation is not below my bid. Only noise traders can sell to me.
- At 0, noise sells with probability about 0.187, for an expected gain of about 0.8 × 0.187 × 6.25 ≈ 0.93.
- At 1, the expected gain is about 0.95, minus about 0.075 lost to informed sellers, giving 0.88.

So a bid of 0 is better.
