game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 8 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 2 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 13, 1 card worth 14. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Fair value before any reveal is about **8.68**. I'm quoting **6.7 / 10.9** around it.

**Fair value.** The deck is {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14}, and there are 28 equally likely two-card hands.
- The minimum is 2 in 7 of them (any hand containing the 2).
- The minimum is 9 in 11 of them: one 9-9 hand, plus each 9 paired with one of the five cards worth 13 or 14.
- The minimum is 13 in 10 of them (any pair drawn from the 13s and the 14).

So the expected value is (7×2 + 11×9 + 10×13) / 28 = 243 / 28 ≈ 8.68.

**Spread.**
- **Informed traders:** they hurt me when the value is 2 (they sell to me at my bid) or 13 (they buy from me at my ask).
- **Noise traders:** their noise has a standard deviation of 6.3, so a quote about 2.2 away from fair value on each side still gets a fair amount of noise flow.
- **Result:** I'm quoting slightly asymmetric, roughly 2.0 below fair value and 2.2 above it.

{"bid": 6.7, "ask": 10.9}

The settlement value is the smaller of two cards drawn from {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14}. There are 28 equally likely pairs.

**Prior distribution**
- Minimum is 2 in 7 pairs (every pair containing the 2).
- Minimum is 9 in 11 pairs.
- Minimum is 13 in 10 pairs.
- The prior expected value is 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Update from the buy at 10.9**
- An informed trader buys at 10.9 only if the value is 13.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(noise > 2.22) ≈ 0.36.
- So the chance of a buy is about 0.49 if the value is 13, and about 0.29 otherwise.
- The posterior weights are 2.03 on 2, 3.19 on 9 and 4.9 on 13.
- The new fair value is about 9.53.

I'll quote around 9.5 with a wide spread, since a wrongly priced trade can cost a lot. I'll skew slightly upward because I'm short 1.

{"bid": 7.6, "ask": 11.6}

Card 1 is 13, so the contract settles at the smaller of 13 and card 2.

**Fair value.** Seven cards remain: 2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 14.
- Settlement is 2 with probability 1/7.
- Settlement is 9 with probability 2/7.
- Settlement is 13 with probability 4/7 (card 2 being 13 or 14 both give 13).
- Expected value is 72/7 ≈ 10.29.

**Ask.** Settlement can never be above 13. So an ask just below 13 loses only 0.1 per trade to informed buyers. Meanwhile it earns about 2.6 per trade from noise buyers, who exceed it about 34% of the time.
- Ask at 12.9: expected edge is about +0.7.
- Ask at 12.0: expected edge is about +0.42, so it is worse.

**Bid.** I compared bids by expected noise profit minus informed loss:

| Bid | Net expected edge |
|---|---|
| 8.5 | about +0.38 |
| 7.0 | about +0.65 |
| 6.5 | about +0.69 |

A bid below 9 is only hit by an informed seller when settlement is 2, so the informed cost is small. The edge is fairly flat around 6.5 to 7, so I'll bid about 6.8.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 12.9}

The first revealed card is 13, so the contract settles at the smaller of 13 and card 2. The remaining 7 cards are {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 14}. That gives a settlement of 2 with probability 1/7, 9 with probability 2/7, and 13 with probability 4/7. Fair value is 72/7 ≈ 10.3.

**Ask side.** Any ask below 13 gets lifted by an informed trader whenever the value is 13, which happens 4/7 of the time. Above 13, no informed trader ever buys, so only noise traders trade. I estimated expected profit at a few asks:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 12.9 | about 0.70 |
| 14 | about 0.82 |
| 15 | about 0.85 |

I'll quote the ask at 15.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells to me only when the value is 2 (1/7). For noise traders, a wider bid earns more per trade but trades less often:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 8.9 | about 0.26 |
| 7 | about 0.65 |
| 5 to 6 | about 0.75 |

I'll quote the bid at 5.5.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 15.0}

game.title: Dice/cards product
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the product of the two dice.

info.raw:
The expected settlement value is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25. The product of two dice is widely spread, with a standard deviation of about 8.9. Informed traders know the exact value, so a tight spread would let them pick me off. I'll quote fairly wide, roughly symmetric around 12.25. That still leaves room to trade with noise traders, whose valuations spread about 6.7 either side of the fair value.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 18.0}

The contract's expected value is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25. The last quote of 6.5 / 18 did not trade, which tells us little, so fair value stays near 12.25.

The settlement value is spread widely, anywhere from 1 to 36. That creates a real risk from informed traders. About 14 in 36 outcomes have a product of 6 or less, so they will often sell to me when the true value is below my bid.

To protect against that, I'll keep a wide spread around 12.25, slightly tighter than last time to catch some noise-trader flow.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 17.5}

A buy at my 17.5 ask is evidence the value is high, so I'm moving my estimate up from the 12.25 prior to about 17.

**Prior.** The product of two dice averages 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25. Only 10 of the 36 outcomes exceed 17.5: 18, 20, 24, 25, 30 and 36. Their average is 24.5.

**Who buys at 17.5:**
- An informed trader buys only when the value is one of those 10 high outcomes. The chance of that is 0.35 × 10/36 ≈ 0.097.
- A noise trader buys when its noise exceeds 17.5 − 12.25 = 5.25, which is 0.78 standard deviations. The chance of that is 0.65 × 0.218 ≈ 0.142.
- So the total chance of a buy is about 0.239.

**Updated estimate.** Given a buy:
- It came from an informed trader with probability 0.097/0.239 ≈ 0.41. Then the expected value is 24.5.
- It came from a noise trader with probability 0.59. Then the expected value stays at 12.25.
- The weighted mean is 0.41 × 24.5 + 0.59 × 12.25 ≈ 17.2.

**Quote.** Payoffs are very uncertain and informed traders are common, so I'll keep the spread wide around 17. I'm already short one unit, so I'll keep the ask a bit higher.

{"bid": 12.5, "ask": 22}

Die 1 = 3, so the contract settles at 3 × die 2. The possible values are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18, each equally likely. Fair value is 10.5.

**Choosing the ask:**
- At 16, an informed trader only buys if the value is 18. That has probability 1/6 and costs 2 per trade, so the expected informed loss is 0.35 × 1/6 × 2 ≈ 0.12.
- A noise trader buys if their valuation is above 16, which has probability about 21%. Each such trade earns about 5.5, so the expected noise gain is 0.65 × 0.21 × 5.5 ≈ 0.74.
- The net is about +0.62. That is better than the alternatives I checked:
  - An ask of 15.1 nets about +0.56.
  - An ask of 18.1 nets about +0.64 gross, with no informed losses.
  - An ask of 12.1 loses money, because informed traders buy whenever the value is 15 or 18.

**Choosing the bid:** The setup is symmetric around 10.5, so a bid of 5 works the same way. An informed trader only sells if the value is 3, losing me 2.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 16}

Fair value is now about 8.2, so I quote bid 4 and ask 12.1.

**Fair value.** With die 1 = 3, the contract settles at one of 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18, each equally likely before trading.

On quote 4 the counterparty sold to me at 5. That tells us something:
- An informed trader would sell at 5 only if the value were 3.
- A noise trader sells at 5 with probability about 0.21. Its fair value was 10.5 and its noise has standard deviation 6.7.
- So the chance of that sale was 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.21 ≈ 0.48 if the value is 3. For any other value it was 0.65 × 0.21 ≈ 0.13.

Updating on this gives a probability of about 0.42 that the value is 3, and about 0.116 for each of the other five values. The fair value is 0.42 × 3 + 0.116 × (6 + 9 + 12 + 15 + 18) ≈ 8.2.

**Ask.** An ask of 12.1 loses only to informed buyers when the value is 15 or 18. Its expected edge is about +0.35 per quote. A tighter ask of 9.5 also loses when the value is 12, and comes out slightly negative.

**Bid.** A bid of 4 loses only to informed sellers when the value is 3, by 1 per unit. Its expected edge is about +0.57, better than bidding 5.9 (about +0.12) or 3.5 (about +0.67 but with fewer trades at a worse price, roughly equal).

{"bid": 4, "ask": 12.1}

Die 1 is 3, so the contract settles at 3 × die 2. The possible values are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18. Before stage 2's trades each was equally likely, with a mean of 10.5.

**Updating on stage 2 trading**
- **Quote 4 (sold to me at my bid of 5):** an informed trader sells there only if the value is 3. A noise trader sells there with probability about 0.21. This raises the chance that the value is 3, and the public fair value falls to about 8.2.
- **Quote 5 (no trade at 4 / 12.1):** an informed trader does not trade only if the value is 6, 9 or 12. A noise trader does not trade with probability about 0.46.
- **Posterior:**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 3 | about 0.30 |
| 6, 9, 12 | about 0.18 each |
| 15, 18 | about 0.08 each |

The fair value is about 8.5.

**Quote**
I bid 5.9, just below 6, so only an informed trader holding a value of 3 sells to me. Their loss to me is outweighed by noise sellers, who sell with probability about 0.35 at about 2.6 below fair value.

I ask 12.1, just above 12, so only informed traders holding 15 or 18 buy from me. Noise buyers, who buy with probability about 0.29 at about 3.6 above fair value, more than cover that cost.

Both sides have positive expected value.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 12.1}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 3.55. I set the bid at 2.0, where noise-trader gains slightly outweigh losses to informed sellers. I set the ask at 8.0, because cheaper asks lose too much to informed buyers holding a 9 or 14.

**Settlement distribution.** The contract is the minimum of 3 cards dealt from 12, so there are C(12,3) = 220 possible hands.
- The minimum is at least 3 in 165 hands, at least 9 in 35 hands, and 14 in 4 hands.
- So the settlement is 1 with probability 55/220 (25%), 3 with 130/220 (59%), 9 with 31/220 (14%) and 14 with 4/220 (2%).
- The expected value is 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Bid.** An informed trader sells to me only when the value is 1, which happens 25% of the time.
- At a bid of 2.6, my expected loss to informed sellers is about 0.20. My expected gain from noise sellers is about 0.175, so the bid loses slightly.
- At a bid of 2.0, the loss to informed sellers is about 0.125. The gain from noise sellers is about 0.22, so the bid is positive.

**Ask.** An informed trader buys from me only when the value is 9 or 14, which happens about 16% of the time.
- At an ask of 5, I expect to lose about 0.36 to informed buyers and gain about 0.22 from noise buyers, so it loses.
- At an ask of 7.5 the two roughly cancel, about 0.16 each way.
- I set the ask at 8, slightly above that break-even point, to stay on the safe side.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

The expected value of the minimum card is about 3.55, so I'm quoting a bid of 2.2 and an ask of 5.5 around it.

**Distribution of the minimum of the 3 dealt cards** (there are C(12,3) = 220 possible hands):

| Minimum | Count | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | ≈ 25% |
| 3 | 130 | ≈ 59% |
| 9 | 31 | ≈ 14% |
| 14 | 4 | ≈ 2% |

The expected value is 780 / 220 ≈ 3.55.

**Bid side.** An informed counterparty sells to me only when the minimum is 1, about 25% of the time, and I lose about 1.2 each time. Noise traders sell below the bid fairly often, and I gain about 1.3 or more on average each time. A bid of 2.2 is reasonable.

**Ask side.** An informed counterparty buys only when the minimum is 9 or 14, about 16% of the time, and I lose about 5 each time. Setting the ask at 5.5 keeps a decent share of noise-trader buys, gaining about 2 each, while limiting that informed loss.

{"bid": 2.2, "ask": 5.5}

Card 1 = 9, so the settlement is min(9, card 2, card 3). The remaining 11 cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.

**Prior over the two unseen cards (55 equally likely pairs):**

| Outcome | How it happens | Pairs | Probability |
|---|---|---|---|
| min = 1 | the 1 is dealt | 10 | 10/55 |
| min = 3 | no 1, at least one 3 | 30 | 30/55 |
| min = 9 | no 1 and no 3 | 15 | 15/55 |

The prior expected value is 235/55 ≈ 4.27.

**Update for the trade at 2.2:** in stage 1 a counterparty sold to me at 2.2.
- An informed trader would only sell there if the value were 1.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 0.21, using a stage-1 fair value near 4.5.
- So the sale is about 5.8 times more likely when the minimum is 1.

**Posterior:**

| Outcome | Probability |
|---|---|
| min = 1 | ≈ 0.56 |
| min = 3 | ≈ 0.29 |
| min = 9 | ≈ 0.15 |

The fair value is about 2.75.

**Quote:** the possible values are clustered at 1, 3 and 9, so informed traders hurt most on the upside. I'll set a fairly wide quote around 2.75. Being long 1 unit is acceptable.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 4.5}

Fair value is now about 2.4, so I'm skewing the quote to sell down my long position.

**Prior with card 1 = 9.** The remaining 11 cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. The settlement is the minimum of 9 and the next two cards.
- P(a 1 is among them) = 2/11, giving a value of 1.
- P(both cards are 9 or higher) = 3/11, giving a value of 9.
- Otherwise there is a 3 and no 1, with probability 6/11, giving a value of 3.
- The expected value is 47/11 ≈ 4.27.

**Update on the sale at 1.2.** A counterparty sold to me at a bid of 1.2.
- If the value is 1, an informed trader sells, so the chance of that sale is about 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.14 ≈ 0.57.
- If the value is 3 or 9, only a noise trader would sell, with a chance of about 0.07.
- The posterior is roughly 65% on a value of 1, 23% on 3 and 12% on 9.
- That gives a fair value of about 2.4.

**Quote.** I hold +2, so I want to sell. I'll set the ask near fair value at 2.8. I'll set the bid at 0.9, below 1, so an informed seller holding a value of 1 won't sell to me.

{"bid": 0.9, "ask": 2.8}

Card 2 is a 1, and the deck has only one 1. So the minimum, and the settlement value, is certain to be 1. The public fair value is 1 as well, because everyone can see the reveal.

That means:
- **Informed traders** value the contract at exactly 1, so they will not trade with a quote that avoids 1 on both sides.
- **Noise traders** value it at 1 plus noise with standard deviation 2.8. Each trade with them earns my distance from 1 times the chance they cross.

The expected edge is roughly x·P(Z > x/2.8). This is maximised at about x ≈ 0.75 × 2.8 ≈ 2.1.

- **Ask:** 1 + 2.1 = 3.1. A sale here earns about 2.1 against settlement and also cuts my long position.
- **Bid:** 1 − 2.1 = −1.1. Prices are not stated to be floored at zero, so I quote symmetrically. A fill here earns about 2.1 and takes me to +3, which is within the limit.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 9.09, so I'm quoting 7.9 / 10.3.

**How I got the fair value**

1. **Larger of dice 1 and 2.** If die 2 shows 12 (probability 1/4), the larger is 12. Otherwise die 2 shows 4, 6 or 7:
   - Half the time die 1 shows 2 or 4, so the larger is die 2's value. That gives 4, 6 and 7 at 1/8 each.
   - The other half die 1 shows 8, so the larger is 8, with total probability 3/8.
   - The expected value of this larger number is 8.125.
2. **Bring in die 3.**
   - Die 3 shows 0, 1 or 2 (probability 0.6): it never beats the first two, so the expected maximum stays 8.125.
   - Die 3 shows 6 (probability 0.1): the 4 is lifted to 6, giving 8.375.
   - Die 3 shows 9 (probability 0.1): everything except 12 becomes 9, giving 9.75.
   - Die 3 shows 12 (probability 0.2): the maximum is 12.
3. **Combine.** E[max] = 0.6×8.125 + 0.1×8.375 + 0.1×9.75 + 0.2×12 ≈ 9.09.

**Spread**

There is a lot of uncertainty about the settlement value, and 20% of counterparties are informed. I'm quoting about 1.2 on each side of fair value to cover that.

{"bid": 7.9, "ask": 10.3}

No information has been revealed yet, and the last quote did not trade, so the fair value is still the unconditional expected maximum of the three dice. I quote around it with a modest spread to cover the 20% chance of an informed trader.

**Fair value**

Maximum of dice 1 and 2 (16 equally likely pairs):

| Max | 4 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Count out of 16 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 6 | 4 |

This gives an expected value of 130/16 = 8.125.

Now fold in die 3:
- **Die 3 is 0, 1 or 2 (prob 0.6):** it never changes the maximum, so the expectation stays 8.125.
- **Die 3 is 6 (prob 0.1):** a maximum of 4 becomes 6, giving 134/16 = 8.375.
- **Die 3 is 9 (prob 0.1):** every maximum below 9 becomes 9, giving 156/16 = 9.75.
- **Die 3 is 12 (prob 0.2):** the maximum is 12.

Expected settlement = 0.6 × 8.125 + 0.1 × 8.375 + 0.1 × 9.75 + 0.2 × 12 ≈ **9.09**.

**Quote**

The last quote at 7.9 / 10.3 drew no trade. I tighten it slightly to attract noise traders, keeping it centred near 9.1.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 10.2}

The third die showed 1, which is below every face on dice 1 and 2. So the contract now settles at the larger of die 1 and die 2.

**Expected value of the larger of die 1 and die 2**
- If die 1 is 2 or 4, the result equals die 2's face: 4, 6, 7 or 12. The average is 7.25.
- If die 1 is 8, the result is 8, 8, 8 or 12. The average is 9.
- Each die 1 face has probability 1/4, so the expected value is (7.25 + 7.25 + 9 + 9) / 4 = **8.125**.
- The counterparty who sold to me at 8 might have been informed, which hints at a lower value. I shade fair value down slightly to about 8.0.

**Placing the quote**
- The only possible settlement values are 4, 6, 7, 8 and 12.
- A bid of 6.8 sits below 7, so an informed seller only hits it when the value is 4 or 6.
- An ask of 9.0 sits above 8, so an informed buyer only lifts it when the value is 12.
- I am long 1 unit, so I lean the bid down a little to slow further buying.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 9.0}

Fair value is about 8.7. I'll quote a bid of 7.6 and an ask of 9.8 around it.

1. **Prior:** Die 3 came up 1, so the contract settles at the larger of die 1 and die 2.
   - If die 1 is 2, the max is 4, 6, 7 or 12, totalling 29.
   - If die 1 is 4, the max is 4, 6, 7 or 12, totalling 29.
   - If die 1 is 8 (two faces), the max is 8, 8, 8 or 12, totalling 36 each time.
   - Over the 16 equally likely combinations the total is 130, so the expected value is 130/16 ≈ 8.13.

2. **Update from the buy at 9:** Only a settlement of 12 is above 9, and 4 of the 16 combinations give 12 (prior 0.25).
   - A noise trader buys at 9 with probability about 0.37.
   - If the value is 12, the chance of a buy is 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.37 ≈ 0.50.
   - Otherwise it is 0.8 × 0.37 ≈ 0.30.
   - So the probability of 12 rises to about 0.36.
   - The other 12 combinations average (130 − 48)/12 ≈ 6.83.
   - Fair value ≈ 0.36 × 12 + 0.64 × 6.83 ≈ 8.7.

3. **Quote:** I'm flat, so I set a symmetric spread of about 1.1 either side of 8.7.

{"bid": 7.6, "ask": 9.8}

With die 3 = 1 and die 1 = 8 revealed, the settlement is max(8, die 2). Die 2 is one of 4, 6, 7 or 12, each equally likely. So the contract settles at 8 with probability 3/4 and at 12 with probability 1/4. Fair value is 9.

**Bid side**
- The settlement can never be below 8. An informed trader therefore never sells to me at any bid of 8 or lower, so only noise traders (valuation 9 plus Normal noise, sd 2.6) hit my bid.
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise valuation below bid) × (9 − bid).
  - Bid 8: 0.8 × 0.35 × 1 ≈ 0.28
  - Bid 7.5: 0.8 × 0.28 × 1.5 ≈ 0.34
  - Bid 7: 0.8 × 0.22 × 2 ≈ 0.35
- A bid of 7 gives the highest expected profit.

**Ask side**
- An informed trader buys whenever the value is 12, which happens with probability 0.2 × 0.25 = 0.05. Each such trade loses me (12 − ask).
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise valuation above ask) × (ask − 9) − 0.05 × (12 − ask).
  - Ask 10.5: ≈ 0.26
  - Ask 11: ≈ 0.30
  - Ask 11.5: 0.8 × 0.168 × 2.5 − 0.05 × 0.5 ≈ 0.31
  - Ask 12: ≈ 0.30
- An ask of 11.5 is the best of these.

My position is −1, so I can still buy or sell one unit within the ±5 limit.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.5}

Die 3 = 1 and die 1 = 8 are revealed, so the contract settles at the larger of 8 and die 2. That gives 8 if die 2 is 4, 6 or 7, and 12 if die 2 is 12. Before any trading, the chance of 12 is 1/4, so the value is worth 9.

**Reading the last trade.** Someone bought at 11.5. A noise trader centred near 9 bids that high only about 17% of the time. An informed trader buys whenever the value is 12.
- If the value is 12, the chance of that buy is 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.17 ≈ 0.33.
- If the value is 8, the chance is 0.8 × 0.17 ≈ 0.13.

Updating on this, the chance the value is 12 rises to about 0.45. Fair value is therefore about 8 + 4 × 0.45 ≈ 9.8.

**Bid at 8.0.** The value can never be below 8, so an informed trader will never sell to me there. A noise trader sells about 24% of the time, giving me roughly 1.8 of expected edge on each such trade.

**Ask at 11.9.** Selling just under 12 means an informed buyer costs me only 0.1, and only when the value is 12. Noise buyers still trade about 21% of the time. The expected gain is about 0.35, better than an ask at 11, which comes to about 0.22.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 11.9}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 10.
- Die 2 (4 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/10), 3 (prob 3/10), 4 (prob 1/5), 5 (prob 2/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dice.

info.raw:
The fair value is about 2.175. I'm quoting a wide spread around it, bid 1.2 and ask 3.2, because about a third of counterparties know the true settlement value.

**Expected value of the contract.** Die 1's faces are 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 10, each with probability 1/8. For each value of die 2, the expected minimum is:

| Die 2 | Probability | Minimums over die 1's faces | Expected minimum |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1/10 | all 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 3/10 | 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3 | 16/8 = 2.000 |
| 4 | 1/5 | 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4 | 19/8 = 2.375 |
| 5 | 2/5 | 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 5 | 22/8 = 2.750 |

Weighting by die 2's probabilities gives 0.3 × 2 + 0.2 × 2.375 + 0.4 × 2.75 = 2.175.

**Why a wide spread.** The settlement value is very spread out. It is 0 with probability 0.1 + 0.9 × 0.25 = 0.325, and it can be as high as 5. Informed traders arrive with probability 0.35, so a tight quote would be picked off often.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 3.2}

Expected settlement value with nothing revealed:

- **Die 1 = 0** (probability 2/8): the minimum is 0.
- **Die 1 = 2** (probability 2/8): the minimum is 0 with probability 0.1, otherwise 2. Average 1.8.
- **Die 1 = 3** (probability 1/8): the minimum is 0 with probability 0.1, otherwise 3. Average 2.7.
- **Die 1 = 5 or 10** (probability 3/8): the minimum equals die 2. Average 0.9 + 0.8 + 2.0 = 3.7.

So E[min] = 0.45 + 0.3375 + 1.3875 ≈ **2.18**. The no-trade at quote 1 tells us little, so fair value stays near 2.2.

The value is 0 with probability about 0.325. That makes informed sellers dangerous, so I lower the bid slightly. Values above 3.2 occur with probability about 0.225 and average about 4.6, so I keep the ask at 3.2.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 3.2}

With die 2 revealed as 5, the contract settles at min(die 1, 5). Die 1's eight faces then give 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 5, so the public fair value is 22/8 = 2.75.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer only lifts my ask when the value is 5, which has probability 3/8.
- At an ask of 5, informed traders never lift, because their valuation of 5 is not above the ask. Noise traders buy with probability about 0.106, which is P(z > 1.25).
- Expected profit at 5 is 0.65 × 0.106 × 2.25 ≈ 0.155. This beat the other asks I tried: about 0.12 at 4.5 and 0.14 at 5.2.

**Bid side.** An informed seller only hits my bid when the value is below it.
- At a bid of 0, informed traders never sell. Noise traders sell with probability about 0.063.
- Expected profit at 0 is 0.65 × 0.063 × 2.75 ≈ 0.113.
- Bids of 0.2 and 0.5 come out about the same or slightly worse, at roughly 0.11 each.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 5}

Die 2 is 5, so the contract settles at min(die 1, 5). Die 1 then gives 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 5, each with probability 1/8. Fair value is 22/8 = 2.75.

**Ask side.** Expected profit per quote, with N(·) the normal tail and noise sd 1.8:
- Informed traders (0.35) buy only when the value is above the ask. The highest possible value is 5, so an ask of 5.0 is never lifted by an informed trader.
- Noise traders (0.65) buy when 2.75 + noise > 5.0, which happens with probability about 10.6%. Each such trade earns 2.25.
- Expected profit is 0.65 × 0.106 × 2.25 ≈ 0.155.
- This beats 4.9 (≈0.151) and 5.2 (≈0.138). An ask of 3.2 loses money, about −0.12.

**Bid side.**
- At a bid of 0.2, informed traders sell only when the value is 0, which has probability 2/8. The loss is 0.35 × 0.25 × 0.2 ≈ 0.018.
- Noise traders sell with probability about 7.8%, earning 2.55 each, for about 0.129.
- Net is about +0.11. This is about the same as a bid of 0 or 0.5, and better than higher bids.

{"bid": 0.2, "ask": 5.0}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 22 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 3, 4 cards worth 4, 4 cards worth 5, 2 cards worth 12, 4 cards worth 13, 3 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Expected minimum of 3 cards ≈ 3.77. The settlement value is most likely between 2 and 5, with a small tail toward 12 or more. I'm quoting a spread wide enough to limit losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 4.8}

The fair value is about 3.77. The last quote produced no trade, so I'm keeping a similar spread around that value.

**Expected minimum of the 3 dealt cards.** For each threshold k, the chance that all three cards are at least k is C(number of cards worth at least k, 3) / C(22, 3). There are 1540 possible deals, since C(22, 3) = 1540.

| Threshold | Cards at or above | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| min ≥ 3 | 20 | 1140/1540 ≈ 0.740 |
| min ≥ 4 | 17 | 680/1540 ≈ 0.442 |
| min ≥ 5 | 13 | 286/1540 ≈ 0.186 |
| min ≥ 6 up to ≥ 12 (7 thresholds) | 9 | 84/1540 ≈ 0.0545 each, 0.382 in total |
| min ≥ 13 | 7 | 35/1540 ≈ 0.023 |
| min ≥ 14 and ≥ 15 | 3 | 1/1540 each, 0.001 in total |

E[min] = 2 + (sum of these probabilities) ≈ 2 + 1.773 ≈ **3.77**.

**Quote.** The last quote (2.8 / 4.8) did not trade, so public fair value has not moved. I'll tighten slightly around 3.77 to pick up more noise-trader flow. The spread of about 0.9 on each side should still cover the 20% chance of facing an informed trader.

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 4.7}

Card 1 is a 4, so the contract settles at 4 unless card 2 or card 3 is lower.

**Fair value.** The other 21 cards are 2×2, 3×3, 3×4, 4×5, 2×12, 4×13 and 3×15. Cards 2 and 3 are two draws from these 21.
- Settles at 2 if either card is a 2: 1 − C(19,2)/C(21,2) = 1 − 171/210 ≈ 0.186
- Settles at 3 if there is no 2 but at least one 3: 171/210 − C(16,2)/C(21,2) = (171 − 120)/210 ≈ 0.243
- Settles at 4 otherwise: 120/210 ≈ 0.571

Expected value ≈ 2(0.186) + 3(0.243) + 4(0.571) ≈ 3.39. Last stage a counterparty sold to me at 2.9, which hints slightly lower. I put fair value at about 3.35.

**Quote.** An informed seller only sells when the value is 2 or 3. An informed buyer only buys when the value is 4.
- A bid of 2.7 loses 0.7 to an informed seller if the value is 2. It gains 0.3 if the value is 3.
- An ask of 3.8 loses only 0.2 to an informed buyer, since the most it can be worth is 4.
- I am already long 1, so I shade both sides slightly down to lean towards selling.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 3.8}

Card 1 is 4, so the contract settles at 4 unless card 2 or card 3 is lower. Twenty-one cards remain, and 2 are drawn from them.

- **P(min = 2):** at least one 2 is drawn. This is 1 − C(19,2)/C(21,2) = 1 − 171/210 ≈ 0.186.
- **P(min = 3):** no 2 is drawn, but at least one 3 is. This is (171 − 120)/210 ≈ 0.243.
- **P(min = 4):** no 2 and no 3 is drawn. This is 120/210 ≈ 0.571.

The fair value is 2(0.186) + 3(0.243) + 4(0.571) ≈ 3.39.

**Ask at 4.0:** settlement can't be above 4, so an informed trader never buys at 4.0. Every trade on that side comes from a noise trader and earns about 0.6.

**Bid at 2.9:** an informed trader only sells here when the value is 2, which happens about 19% of the time. Pricing the bid slightly low also reduces my risk, since I'm already long 1.

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 4.0}

Card 3 is drawn from the 20 cards left in the deck. Card 1 and card 2 are both 4, so the contract settles at 4 unless card 3 is lower.

- **Settlement value:** 2 with probability 2/20, 3 with probability 3/20, and 4 with probability 15/20.
- **Fair value:** 0.2 + 0.45 + 3.0 = 3.65.

**Ask:** The informed trader buys only if its value of 4 is above my ask. Any ask of 4.0 or higher means it never buys, so only noise traders buy from me. Expected profit per quote, counting only the 0.8 chance of a noise trader:

| Ask | Profit if filled | Chance noise buys | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.3 | 0.65 | 0.39 | 0.25 × 0.8 = 0.20 |
| 4.8 | 1.15 | 0.31 | 0.36 × 0.8 = 0.29 |
| 4.9 | 1.25 | 0.29 | 0.36 × 0.8 = 0.29 |
| 5.5 | 1.85 | 0.15 | 0.28 × 0.8 = 0.22 |

The best range is about 4.7 to 4.9, so I ask 4.8. Being long 2 also makes a sale welcome.

**Bid:** At 2.6, a noise trader sells with probability about 0.32 and I gain 1.05, worth about 0.27. The informed trader only sells when the value is 2, so I lose 0.6 with probability 0.2 × 0.1, which costs about 0.012. A bid of 2.5 trades slightly less often but makes buying a third unit cheaper, so I bid 2.5.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 4.8}

Remaining 20 cards: 2×2, 3×3, 2×4, 4×5, and 9 high cards.
Settlement is min(4, card 3):
- 2 with probability 2/20
- 3 with probability 3/20
- 4 otherwise, probability 15/20

Expected value = (4 + 9 + 60)/20 = 3.65.

Trading history may shift the public fair value a little, but 3.65 is a reasonable estimate.

The settlement value is at most 4, so an informed trader never buys above 4. Any ask at or above 4 will only fill with noise traders, and each such sale earns at least ask − 3.65. Expected profit per quote is about 0.8 × P(noise valuation > a) × (a − 3.65).
- At a = 4.6: (0.95)(1 − Φ(0.413)) ≈ 0.95 × 0.34 ≈ 0.32.
- At a = 5.0: 1.35 × 0.28 ≈ 0.38.
- At a = 5.5: 1.85 × 0.21 ≈ 0.39.
- At a = 5.8: 2.15 × 0.175 ≈ 0.38.

Profit is roughly flat between 5.0 and 5.8, so I'll quote an ask of about 5.4.

{"bid": null, "ask": 5.4}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 1/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is about 48.8, but the outcome is split into two groups, so I'm quoting a wide spread with an asymmetric ask.

**Expected value.** The chance of heads averages 0.4·0.3 + 0.1·0.4 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.61. That gives 8 × 0.61 × 10 ≈ 48.8.

**Shape of the outcome.**
- If the coin is the 0.9 coin, the settlement is usually 70–80.
- Otherwise it is usually 20–30.
- So the value is rarely near the 48.8 average.

**Ask side.** I compared ask prices by weighing profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders.
- At 65, the expected gain is about +1.1 per quote. Informed traders hit it whenever the high-bias coin was picked (value 70 or more).
- At 70–72, the expected gain is about +2.1 to +2.3. Informed traders only hurt me when the result is 80 (eight heads), which happens about 21% of the time.
- 72 scored best of the prices I tried, so I use it.

**Bid side.** Informed traders sell to me when the value is 20 or below, which happens about 25% of the time.
- A bid of 28 gives about +1.7. A bid of 25 also gives about +1.7.
- I use 26, between the two.

{"bid": 26, "ask": 72}

Prior expected value: the coin's average heads probability is 0.61, so 8 flips × 0.61 × 10 = 48.8.

**What the last trade tells me.** A counterparty sold to me at 26.
- An informed trader sells only if the true value is below 26, which means 2 or fewer heads.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 0.19 (a valuation 0.88 standard deviations below 48.8).

**Updated coin probabilities.** I weighted each coin by how likely it was to produce that sale:
- Coin with P(heads) = 0.3: about 0.60 (was 0.40)
- Coin with P(heads) = 0.4: about 0.11 (was 0.10)
- Coin with P(heads) = 0.9: about 0.29 (was 0.50)

This gives an average heads probability of about 0.485, so roughly 39. The sale also suggests few heads even for a given coin, which pulls the value down a bit further, to about 36.

**Quote.** I'm already long one unit, and the value is bimodal (low coins average about 25, the high coin about 72). So I'll keep the spread wide and centre it slightly below 36: bid 22, ask 50.

{"bid": 22, "ask": 50}

Fair value is about 60, so I'm quoting 48 / 68 around it.

**Posterior on the coin after 3 heads in 4 flips.** The likelihood of this result is p³(1−p).

| Coin P(heads) | Prior | Likelihood | Prior × likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.4 | 0.0189 | 0.00756 | 0.158 |
| 0.4 | 0.1 | 0.0384 | 0.00384 | 0.080 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.0729 | 0.03645 | 0.762 |

**Expected settlement.**
- The expected heads probability is 0.158 × 0.3 + 0.080 × 0.4 + 0.762 × 0.9 ≈ 0.765.
- That gives about 3.06 heads expected in the 4 unrevealed flips.
- With the 3 heads already shown, the expected total is 6.06 heads, so the contract is worth about 60.6.

**Adjustment for the trade history.** Both earlier counterparties sold to me, at 26 and 22. An informed seller at those prices would imply a low settlement value. That nudges my fair value down slightly, to about 58–60.

**Risk on each side.** If the coin is the 0.9 one, settlement will be roughly 50–70, so informed buyers are the main danger above fair. If it is a 0.3 or 0.4 coin, settlement is about 30–50, so informed sellers are the danger below. I'm already long 2, so I keep the bid wider below fair than the ask is above it.

{"bid": 48, "ask": 68}

Fair value is about **60.6**, so I'm quoting 51 / 70, which sits about 10 below and 10 above it.

**Updating on the revealed flips.** Flips 1–4 show 3 heads and 1 tail. For each coin, the chance of that result is p³(1−p), weighted by how likely that coin was to be picked:
- P(heads) = 0.3: 0.027 × 0.7 × 0.4 = 0.00756
- P(heads) = 0.4: 0.064 × 0.6 × 0.1 = 0.00384
- P(heads) = 0.9: 0.729 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.03645

These sum to 0.04785. Dividing each by the total gives the updated chances:
- 0.3 coin: about 0.158
- 0.4 coin: about 0.080
- 0.9 coin: about 0.762

**Fair value.**
- The expected chance of heads on each remaining flip is 0.158 × 0.3 + 0.080 × 0.4 + 0.762 × 0.9 ≈ 0.765.
- Four flips remain, so I expect about 3.06 more heads, worth about 30.6.
- The 3 heads already shown are worth 30, so fair value is about 60.6.
- The stage 1 trades say little beyond what the flips now show.

**Spread.** An informed trader could hold a value well away from 60, because the coin and four flips are still unknown. A spread of about ±10 protects against them while still catching noise traders, whose valuations spread by 26. I'm long 2, so the ask is set a little closer to fair than the bid, to make selling slightly more likely.

{"bid": 51, "ask": 70}

With 5 heads in 6 flips, the coin is almost surely the 0.9 coin, so fair value is about 67.5.

**Which coin it is.** I weighted each coin's prior by the chance of seeing 5 heads and 1 tail, which is p⁵(1−p):

| Coin | Prior | Likelihood p⁵(1−p) | Prior × likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| p = 0.3 | 0.4 | 0.0017 | 0.00068 | ≈ 0.022 |
| p = 0.4 | 0.1 | 0.0061 | 0.00061 | ≈ 0.020 |
| p = 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.0590 | 0.0295 | ≈ 0.958 |

**Fair value.**
- The expected heads probability is 0.022 × 0.3 + 0.020 × 0.4 + 0.958 × 0.9 ≈ 0.877.
- That gives about 1.75 expected heads in the last 2 flips.
- Fair value ≈ 50 + 10 × 1.75 = 67.5.

**Possible settlements.** The contract can only settle at 50, 60 or 70:
- 70 has probability about 0.77.
- 60 has probability about 0.20.
- 50 has probability about 0.03.

**Ask at 71.** An informed trader values the contract at 70 at most, so it never buys above 70. Only noise traders hit this ask, and each such sale earns about 3.5 over fair value.

**Bid at 59.** An informed trader only sells to me here if settlement is 50, which happens about 3% of the time. Noise traders selling below 59 give me about 8.5 of edge.

{"bid": 59, "ask": 71}

With 6 flips revealed, the posterior strongly favours the 0.9 coin. That puts fair value near 67.5, and the contract can only settle at 50, 60 or 70.

**Which coin is it?** Five heads and one tail have been revealed so far. The likelihood of that for each coin is p⁵(1−p), weighted by the prior:

| Coin P(heads) | Prior × likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.4 × 0.3⁵ × 0.7 ≈ 0.00068 | ≈ 2.2% |
| 0.4 | 0.1 × 0.4⁵ × 0.6 ≈ 0.00061 | ≈ 2.0% |
| 0.9 | 0.5 × 0.9⁵ × 0.1 ≈ 0.02952 | ≈ 95.8% |

**Fair value.** The expected chance of heads on each remaining flip is about 0.877. Two flips remain, so about 1.75 more heads are expected. That gives a fair value of about 50 + 17.5 = 67.5.

**Settlement odds:**
- 70: about 79%
- 60: about 19%
- 50: about 2%

**Choosing the quote:**
- **Ask 70.** An informed trader only buys if the settlement value is above 70, which is impossible. So only noise traders buy here, and each sale earns about 2.5 above fair value.
- **Bid 60.** An informed trader only sells if the value is below 60, which needs settlement at 50. That has roughly a 2% chance times the 0.35 chance the trader is informed, costing 10 if it happens. Noise traders who sell earn me about 7.5 each.

Both sides have positive expected value.

{"bid": 60, "ask": 70}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description: A custom deck of 20 cards is shuffled: 3 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 4, 1 card worth 5, 4 cards worth 7, 2 cards worth 9, 3 cards worth 10, 3 cards worth 11, 3 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The fair value is the expected highest of the 3 cards dealt, which works out to about 11.98.

**Probability that the highest card is at most v.** This equals the number of ways to deal 3 cards all worth v or less, divided by C(20,3) = 1140.

| v | Cards ≤ v | Ways (out of 1140) | Ways the max equals v |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 3 | 1 | 1 |
| 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 |
| 5 | 5 | 10 | 6 |
| 7 | 9 | 84 | 74 |
| 9 | 11 | 165 | 81 |
| 10 | 14 | 364 | 199 |
| 11 | 17 | 680 | 316 |
| 15 | 20 | 1140 | 460 |

**Expected value.** Multiply each value by the number of ways the max equals it, add them up, and divide by 1140:

3·1 + 4·3 + 5·6 + 7·74 + 9·81 + 10·199 + 11·316 + 15·460 = 13658

13658 / 1140 ≈ 11.98

**Quote.** I'll centre the quote on about 12 and stay 1 point either side. That is wide enough to cover losses to informed traders while still trading with noise traders, whose valuations have a standard deviation of 2.7.

{"bid": 11.0, "ask": 13.0}

The fair value before the trade is the expected maximum of 3 cards drawn from the 20-card deck.

**Expected maximum.** Of the C(20,3) = 1140 possible hands, the number whose maximum is at most v is the number of ways to pick 3 cards worth v or less. Taking differences gives the number of hands whose maximum is exactly v:

| Max card | Hands with this max |
|---|---|
| 3 | 1 |
| 4 | 3 |
| 5 | 6 |
| 7 | 74 |
| 9 | 81 |
| 10 | 199 |
| 11 | 316 |
| 15 | 460 |

Weighting each value by its count gives 13658 / 1140 ≈ 11.98.

**Updating for the trade.** The counterparty bought at 13, which is above the prior value. An informed trader holding a 15 would do this, so the fair value moves up a little, to about 12.2.

**Quote.** I am short 1, so I set the quote slightly asymmetric (11.4 bid, 13.2 ask around ~12.2) to lean toward buying.

{"bid": 11.4, "ask": 13.2}

The deck gives a prior expected maximum of about 11.98, with a 40% chance the maximum is a 15.

Both trades so far were buys at my ask of about 13. An informed counterparty buys there only if the value is 15, so these buys raise that probability. My rough estimate is now about 65%. That puts expected settlement near 13.25.

I'm already short 2. So I'm quoting roughly centred near 13.4 and set wide, to lean against selling more.

{"bid": 12.6, "ask": 14.4}

Card 1 = 15, which is the highest card in the deck. That means the max is 15 for certain, so the settlement value is known to be 15.

Every counterparty, informed or noise, values the contract around 15. Noise traders sit at 15 ± 2.7.

I'm short 2, so I want to buy back. A tight quote, such as a bid of 14.9 and an ask of 15.1, earns spread against noise traders and carries no adverse selection, because the value is known. Buying at 14.9 gains 0.1 per unit, and selling at 15.1 gains 0.1. Hitting the position limit doesn't matter much since every trade is profitable.

I could widen the quote for more edge per trade. If I bid 14 and a trade happens, I gain 1. The probability of a fill is the chance the valuation falls below 14, which is P(z < -0.37) ≈ 0.36. Expected value per side is roughly (15 − b)·Φ((b − 15)/2.7). This is maximized around a distance d where d·φ/2.7 = Φ, which gives d ≈ 2.7·0.75 ≈ 2. At d = 2, Φ(-0.74) ≈ 0.23, so the expected gain is about 0.46 per side. At d = 1.5, Φ(-0.56) ≈ 0.29, so the expected gain is about 0.43. Informed traders at exactly 15 won't trade at either price.

So I'll quote a bid of 13 and an ask of 17.

{"bid": 13, "ask": 17}

Card 1 = 15, which is the maximum value in the deck. So settlement is exactly 15 and there's no uncertainty.

Since the value is known to everyone, informed traders and the fair value are both 15. Noise valuations are 15 ± 2.7. If I buy below 15 I profit, and if I sell above 15 I profit. I'm short 2, but covering below 15 is still profitable.

I'll quote a bid of 14 and an ask of 16. With a symmetric spread, each fill earns 1, and informed traders won't trade against either side.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 16}

Card 1 is a 15, the highest card in the deck, so the settlement value is certain to be 15. Informed traders also value it at 15, so they will not trade against a spread that straddles 15. Only noise traders will trade, and every fill is profit.

To set the width, I balance the profit per fill against how often a fill happens. Noise valuations are 15 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.7.
- A bid at 13 fills about 23% of the time and earns 2 per fill, worth about 0.46.
- A bid at 14 fills more often but earns only 1, worth about 0.36.
- A bid at 12.5 is worth about 0.44, slightly less than 13.

The ask is symmetric, so 17 is also worth about 0.46. A sell there would take my position from -2 to -3, which is still within the limit.

{"bid": 13, "ask": 17}

Card 1 = 15 already, so the max is 15 regardless of card 3. Settlement is known to be 15.

Fair value = 15. Noise traders value 15 + N(0, 2.7). Informed traders value exactly 15, so they never trade against a quote above 15 on the ask or below 15 on the bid.

I am short 2, so I prefer to buy back. Expected profit per trade, using p as the chance a noise trader crosses:
- A bid at 15 − d earns d each time it fills.
- d = 1: P(fill) = 0.8·0.356 ≈ 0.285, so expected profit ≈ 0.285.
- d = 1.5: P(fill) = 0.8·0.289 ≈ 0.231, so ≈ 0.35.
- d = 2: P(fill) = 0.8·0.229 ≈ 0.18, so ≈ 0.37.
- d = 2.5: P(fill) = 0.8·0.177 ≈ 0.14, so ≈ 0.35.

The ask side is symmetric, so I quote about 2 away from 15 on each side. Position limits are not binding: from −2 I can buy up to 5 units or sell 1 more.

{"bid": 13, "ask": 17}

Card 1 is 15, the highest card in the deck, so the contract will settle at exactly 15. Since the settlement value is known, any buy below 15 or sell above 15 locks in profit.

- **Informed traders:** they value the contract at 15, so they never trade against a quote that straddles 15.
- **Noise traders:** their valuations are spread around 15 with standard deviation 2.7.
- **Choosing the spread:** expected profit per side is (distance from 15) × (chance a noise trader crosses that price). This is largest when the distance is about 0.75 × 2.7 ≈ 2.
- **Quote:** that gives a bid of 13 and an ask of 17. Both sides are allowed at my position of -2.

{"bid": 13, "ask": 17}

Card 1 is 15 and 15 is the highest card in the deck, so the maximum is 15 whatever card 3 turns out to be. Settlement is 15 with certainty.

An informed trader values the contract at exactly 15. A noise trader values it at 15 plus noise. To profit, I can sell above 15 and buy below 15.

I'm short 2, so I can still sell one more unit and stay within the limit. I'll quote a tight market around 15: bid 14.6, ask 15.4.

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 15.4}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value is 4.5. That comes from two equally likely coins: the fair coin gives an expected 3 heads, and the two-headed coin always gives 6. The settlement value is 6 a little over half the time (about 0.508). Informed traders will often want to buy, so I'm keeping the spread wide and centred on 4.5.

{"bid": 3.3, "ask": 5.7}

After one buy at my ask, I estimate the public fair value at about 4.9. I'll keep the ask at 6.0 and set the bid at 3.4.

**Prior.** With probability 1/2 the coin always lands heads, so the contract settles at 6. Otherwise it is a fair coin and the count follows Binomial(6, 0.5).
- That gives P(settle = 6) ≈ 0.5 + 1/128 ≈ 0.508.
- The prior mean is 4.5.

**Update from the buy at 5.7.**
- An informed trader buys at 5.7 only if the settlement is 6.
- A noise trader buys if 4.5 plus noise is above 5.7. That needs noise above 1.2, which happens with probability about 0.32.
- If the value is 6, the chance of a buy is 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.32 ≈ 0.46.
- If the value is below 6, the chance of a buy is 0.8 × 0.32 ≈ 0.26.
- So the posterior P(settle = 6) is about 0.647.

**New fair value.** Given a fair coin and a result below 6, the expected head count is about 2.95. The fair value is 0.647 × 6 + 0.353 × 2.95 ≈ 4.9.

**Quote.**
- **Ask at 6.0:** an informed trader can never profit from buying at 6, since 6 is the maximum. Noise traders still buy about a third of the time, so this side is safe.
- **Bid at 3.4:** the settlement value is likely either 6 or around 3, so I keep the bid wide. This limits losses to informed traders when the coin is fair and the count comes out low.

{"bid": 3.4, "ask": 6.0}

The fair value is about 5.6–5.7, and an ask of 6.0 cannot lose to an informed trader.

1. **Which coin is it.** Both revealed flips came up heads.
   - That outcome has probability 1 with the always-heads coin and 0.25 with the fair coin.
   - So the chance the coin is the always-heads one is 0.5×1 / (0.5×1 + 0.5×0.25) = 0.8.

2. **Expected heads in the last 4 flips.** Each remaining flip is heads with probability 0.8×1 + 0.2×0.5 = 0.9. That gives 4 × 0.9 = 3.6 expected heads.

3. **Fair value.** The 2 heads already shown plus 3.6 gives an expected settlement of 5.6. The trader who bought from me at 5.7 points slightly higher, so I take fair value as about 5.6–5.7.

4. **Ask.** The settlement can never be above 6. An ask of 6.0 can never lose money to an informed buyer. Noise traders will still sometimes buy at that price.

5. **Bid.** If the coin is fair, the settlement can be well below fair value. In that case an informed seller would hurt me at a high bid, so I keep the bid wide at 4.6.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 6.0}

Two heads in two flips make the always-heads coin more likely. Before trading, P(always-heads) = 0.8 and P(fair) = 0.2.

**Effect of the buy at 6.** An informed trader buys at 6 only if the settlement value is above 6. That happens with neither coin, since the maximum is 6. So the buy at 6 must have come from a noise trader. Noise traders value around the public fair value, which was about 5.6, so they buy at 6 roughly 44% of the time. Because that chance doesn't depend on which coin it is, the trade tells us nothing. P(always-heads) stays at 0.8.

**Fair value now.**
- Always-heads coin: settles at 6.
- Fair coin: expected 2 + 2 = 4.
- Fair value = 0.8 × 6 + 0.2 × 4 = 5.6.

**Ask.** The settlement value can never exceed 6. An ask of 6.1 can never be hit by an informed trader. Any fill there is a noise trader and gains at least 0.1 per unit even in the worst case. I am short 2, so I have room to sell more.

**Bid.** On a buy, informed sellers have the edge only when it is a fair coin. That leaves the fill worth about 5.36, which is the fair-coin value of 4 given a weight of about 0.36 and the always-heads value of 6 given about 0.64. A bid of 5.0 keeps a positive edge with some margin and helps cover my short.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 6.1}

Four heads in a row make the always-heads coin very likely, so the contract will almost surely settle at 6.

**Posterior on the coin.** The chance of seeing 4 heads with the fair coin is 0.5 × 1/16 = 1/32. With the always-heads coin it is 0.5 × 1 = 1/2. So P(fair coin) = 1/17 and P(always-heads coin) = 16/17.

**Settlement distribution.**
- Value 6: 16/17 + (1/17)(1/4) ≈ 0.956
- Value 5: (1/17)(1/2) ≈ 0.029
- Value 4: (1/17)(1/4) ≈ 0.015
- Expected value ≈ 5.94, which is also the public fair value.

**Informed traders.** Settlement can never exceed 6. With an ask above 6, an informed trader never buys from me. With a bid of 4 or below, an informed trader only sells if the value is below my bid, which never happens. So both sides face no adverse selection.

**Noise traders.** Their valuations are 5.94 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. My profit on one side is roughly the distance from fair value times the chance the noise trader crosses that distance. That is maximised at a distance of about 0.75 × 2.6 ≈ 2 on each side. This gives a bid near 3.9 and an ask near 7.9.

**Position.** I am short 1, so one more trade either way keeps me well within the ±4 limit.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 7.9}

With four heads in four flips, the coin is almost certainly the always-heads coin, so the contract is worth about 5.94.

**Fair value**
- The chance the coin is the always-heads one is 16/17. The fair coin produces four heads only 1/16 of the time.
- If it is the always-heads coin, the contract settles at 6.
- If it is the fair coin, it settles at 4, 5 or 6, averaging 5.
- So the expected value is (16/17 × 6) + (1/17 × 5) ≈ 5.94.
- The most likely outcome is 6, at about 95.6%.

**Quote**
- An informed trader almost surely values the contract at exactly 6. It buys only if its valuation is above my ask, so any ask above 6 is safe from it.
- Against noise traders (fair value plus noise with standard deviation 2.6), the best ask is roughly 2 above fair value, around 7.9.
- The same logic puts the bid about 2 below fair value, around 3.9. An informed trader with value 4 or more will not sell at 3.9, so the bid only fills from noise traders.

game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Before any flips are shown, the fair value is 4.5. It is an even mix of a fair coin (expected 3 heads) and a two-headed coin (6 heads).

- **Ask at 5.5:** informed traders buy only when the value is 6 (about 51% of the time). Each of those trades loses me 0.5. Noise traders buy about 28% of the time, and each of those trades gains me about 1. Overall the ask has positive expected profit.
- **Bid at 3.5:** informed traders sell when the value is 3 or less. That happens about 33% of the time, with an average value near 2.3, so I lose about 1.2 per trade. Noise traders sell about 28% of the time, with a margin of about 1. The noise trades roughly cover the informed losses.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 5.5}

After the sell at 3.5, my updated fair value is about 3.6, so I'm quoting about 1 below it and about 1 above it.

- **Before any trade:** the coin is fair or always heads with equal odds. A fair coin averages 3 heads and the biased coin gives 6, so the starting fair value was 4.5.
- **What the sell tells me:** the counterparty sold to me at 3.5.
  - An informed trader sells there only if the true count is 3 or less, which needs the fair coin.
  - A noise trader sells there with probability about 0.28.
  - Overall, a sell is about 0.18 likely under the biased coin and about 0.41 likely under the fair coin.
- **Updated beliefs:** the chance of the biased coin drops to about 0.31. Given the fair coin and a sell, the expected count is about 2.6. That puts the fair value at about 0.31 × 6 + 0.69 × 2.6 ≈ 3.6.
- **Quote:** a bid of 2.6 and an ask of 4.6 gives a wide spread against informed traders. Both prices sit slightly low because I am long 1 unit and would rather sell than buy more.

{"bid": 2.6, "ask": 4.6}

The quote is centred near a fair value of about 3.6, with a wide 2.1 spread and a slight downward skew because I'm already long.

**Fair value before any trading:** the contract is worth 3 with the fair coin (6 flips × 0.5) and 6 with the double-headed coin. With equal odds, that averages to 4.5.

**Quote 1 (they sold at 3.5):**
- If the coin is fair, the chance of a sell at 3.5 is about 0.41:
  - An informed trader sells when the true count is 3 or less, which happens with probability 42/64.
  - A noise trader sells when its valuation falls below 3.5, which happens with probability 0.28.
- If the coin is double-headed, the value is 6, so an informed trader never sells. The chance of a sell is only 0.65 × 0.28 ≈ 0.18.
- The fair coin is about 2.3 times more likely, so P(fair) rises to about 0.69 and fair value drops to about 3.9.

**Quote 2 (no trade between 2.6 and 4.6):**
- If the coin is fair, the chance of no trade is about 0.48:
  - An informed trader doesn't trade when the true count is 3 or 4, which happens with probability 35/64.
  - A noise trader's valuation lands between 2.6 and 4.6 with probability about 0.44.
- If the coin is double-headed, an informed trader would have bought, so only noise traders produce no trade. That chance is about 0.28.
- The fair coin is about 1.7 times more likely again, so P(fair) is about 0.79 and fair value is about 0.79 × 3 + 0.21 × 6 ≈ 3.6.

**This quote:** I keep the spread wide because 35% of counterparties are informed. I shade the quote slightly down because I'm long one unit.

{"bid": 2.6, "ask": 4.7}

The two revealed tails mean the coin cannot be the always-heads coin, so it is the fair coin. My earlier long came from the 3.5 buy in stage 1, which now looks costly. The past trades tell me nothing new because the coin is now known.

**Fair value:** 0 heads from flips 1–2, plus 4 fair flips still to come. That gives an expected value of 0 + 4 × 0.5 = **2.0**.

**Settlement value is 0 to 4, binomial (4, 0.5):**

| Settlement value | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/16 | 4/16 | 6/16 | 4/16 | 1/16 |

**Adverse selection:** With probability 0.35 the trader knows the exact value. Against a 2.0 mid, an informed trader only trades when the value is 1 or less, or 3 or more. Each of those cases has probability 5/16.

**Spread:** Noise traders' valuations have a standard deviation of 1.7, so quotes about 0.5–0.6 from the mid still trade often. A spread of roughly ±0.55 around 2.0 should earn enough from noise trades to cover losses to informed traders.

**Skew:** I am long 1, so I lean slightly toward selling by keeping the ask a little closer to fair value.

{"bid": 1.4, "ask": 2.5}

The coin must be the fair one, since flip 1 came up tails. The remaining 4 flips follow a Binomial(4, 0.5) distribution, so before the last trade the expected settlement was 2.

**Updating on the buy at 2.5 in quote 4:**
- An informed trader buys at 2.5 only if the settlement value is 3 or more.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(N > 0.29) ≈ 0.385.
- The chance of that buy is about 0.25 if the value is 2 or less, and about 0.60 if it is 3 or more.

**Posterior over the settlement value:**

| Value | Weight |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.016 |
| 1 | 0.063 |
| 2 | 0.094 |
| 3 | 0.150 |
| 4 | 0.038 |

The updated expected settlement is about 2.37.

**Quote:** I centre the quote near 2.37 and widen it to guard against informed traders. Because settlement values are whole numbers, the bid stays above 1 and the ask stays above 3.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 3.1}

Flip 1 is tails, so the coin is fair. That leaves 4 unknown flips, each heads with probability 0.5. Expected settlement = 0 + 4 × 0.5 = 2.

The trades so far carry little information. The counterparty at quote 4 bought at 2.5, so an informed trader would value it at 3 or 4. Quote 5 had no trade, so the value is likely 2 (with the earlier quote, informed could have been 2 or 3).

Rough posterior from the binomial on 4 flips: P(0)=1/16, P(1)=4/16, P(2)=6/16, P(3)=4/16, P(4)=1/16. The buy at 2.5 and the no-trade at quote 5 tilt this slightly upward, so public fair value is about 2.1–2.2.

I'll quote around 2.2:

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 2.9}

The coin must be the fair one, so fair value is **3.0**.

**Fair value.** Flips 1 and 2 came up tails, and the always-heads coin can never show tails. Two heads are already revealed. Flips 5 and 6 are fair, so settlement is:
- 2 with probability 0.25
- 3 with probability 0.5
- 4 with probability 0.25

**Informed traders** value the contract at exactly 2, 3 or 4. A bid at or below 2 never loses to an informed seller. An ask at or above 4 never loses to an informed buyer. So the risk from them is small.

**Noise traders** value it at 3 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7. For a bid at b, expected profit from noise sellers is roughly (3 − b) × P(noise valuation < b). This peaks around b ≈ 1.5, giving about 1.5 × 0.19 ≈ 0.28 per noise trader. A bid at 1.9 gives about 1.1 × 0.26 ≈ 0.29, which is close. The ask works the same way by symmetry.

**Quote.** I'll quote symmetrically around 3: bid 1.5, ask 4.5. My position of +1 is comfortably inside the limits, so it doesn't need a skew.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 4.5}

The settlement value now sits in a narrow range, so I'm quoting just outside it.

**Fair value.** Flip 1 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one. Two heads are already in. The last two flips are fair, so the settlement is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. The fair value is 3.

**Informed traders.** An informed counterparty only hurts me if I sell below 4 or buy above 2. Quoting outside that range means they cannot pick me off.

**Choosing the ask.** Only noise traders buy above 4. Noise valuations are 3 plus normal noise with standard deviation 1.7. My expected profit from the ask is 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 3):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4.1 | about 0.185 |
| 4.3 | about 0.188 |
| 4.5 | about 0.184 |

The ask at 4.3 does best. The bid at 1.7 is the mirror image and earns the same. My position of +1 is no concern with two quotes left.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

- **Heads so far:** 2.
- **Flips 5 and 6:** these are fair flips, so the final total is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4. The fair value is 3.

**Ask side:**

- Expected profit per quote:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4.0 | 0.181 |
| 4.2 | 0.187 |
| 4.4 | 0.186 |

The best ask is about 4.3.

**Bid side:** the situation is symmetric around 3, so the best bid is about 1.7.

- The chance of that sequence is 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 for the fair coin and 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.16 for the 0.8 coin.
- Weighting by the priors gives 0.6 × 0.25 = 0.15 against 0.4 × 0.16 = 0.064.

- That gives about 4.54 heads, or about 22.7 in contract value.

**Adjusting for the trade history.** Counterparties have bought at my ask twice, including at 26 in quote 5. Either could have been an informed trader, so I nudge fair value up to about 23.5.

**Quote.** I'm short 1, so selling one more is acceptable but I shouldn't sell cheaply. I'll quote roughly symmetric around 23.5, with the ask slightly wider.

{"bid": 20.0, "ask": 27.0}

Of the seven revealed flips, four are heads. I weighed the two possible coins by how well each explains that record.
- The chance of this record is 0.5^7 ≈ 0.0078 for the fair coin and 0.8^4 × 0.2^3 ≈ 0.0033 for the biased coin.
- After weighting by the prior odds, the chance the coin is biased is about 0.22.
- The chance flip 8 is heads is 0.5 + 0.3 × 0.22 ≈ 0.566.

Settlement can only be 20 or 25. If I bid just below 20 and ask just above 25, an informed trader never has a reason to trade with me. Noise traders still trade with me often enough at those prices to make a profit. I also checked a tighter bid of 21. It earns less, because informed traders would sell to me whenever the value is 20.

{"bid": 19.9, "ask": 25.1}

Four of the seven revealed flips are heads, so the settlement can only be 20 (flip 8 tails) or 25 (flip 8 heads).

**Which coin is it?**
- If the coin is fair, the chance of these 7 flips is 0.5^7 = 0.00781. Weighted by its 3/5 prior, that gives 0.00469.
- If the coin is biased, the chance is 0.8^4 × 0.2^3 = 0.00328. Weighted by its 2/5 prior, that gives 0.00131.

**Quotes**

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The expected settlement is about 2.58 heads, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it: bid 1.6, ask 3.6.

- **Expected heads:** the average chance of heads is 0.2×0.3 + 0.3×0.4 + 0.5×0.5 = 0.43. Over 6 flips that gives 6 × 0.43 ≈ 2.58.
- **Uncertainty:** the spread of the flips and the uncertainty about which coin it is give a standard deviation of about 1.3 heads.
- **Informed traders:** the settlement value is a whole number, so an informed trader only trades if it lands outside my quotes.
  - With a bid of 1.6, an informed trader sells to me only if the value is 0 or 1.
  - With an ask of 3.6, an informed trader buys from me only if the value is 4 or more.
- **Noise traders:** these traders value the contract at about 2.58 plus noise of 1.3. Some of them will still trade at these prices, and I profit on average from those trades.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 3.6}

After the buy at 3.6, I estimate fair value is about 3.4, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it.

**Before any trades.** The coin's expected heads probability is 0.2×0.3 + 0.3×0.4 + 0.5×0.5 = 0.43. Over 6 flips, that gives an expected 2.58 heads.

**The quote-1 buy at 3.6 means one of two things:**
- **An informed trader:** settlement must be at least 4. With p ≈ 0.43, that happens roughly 20% of the time.
- **A noise trader:** its valuation came out above 3.6. That needs noise of more than about 0.78 standard deviations above 2.58, which happens about 22% of the time.

**Updated fair value.** Each type is equally likely in advance. So the buy came from an informed trader with probability about 0.2 / (0.2 + 0.22) ≈ 0.48. If informed, the expected settlement given at least 4 heads is about 4.4. If noise, it stays about 2.58. The new estimate is 0.48 × 4.4 + 0.52 × 2.58 ≈ 3.45.

**Quote.** Centred near 3.3–3.4, about 1 point each side. That still leaves room for my short position to cover if the price moves up.

{"bid": 2.3, "ask": 4.3}

Settlement is the number of heads in 6 flips, so I priced it from the coin posterior after the revealed tail.

**Updating on flip 1 = tails:**
- p = 0.3: 0.2 × 0.7 = 0.14
- p = 0.4: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18
- p = 0.5: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25

These weights total 0.57, so the posterior mean P(heads) = (0.14·0.3 + 0.18·0.4 + 0.25·0.5) / 0.57 ≈ 0.419.

**Fair value:** Flip 1 is already 0, so only flips 2–6 remain. That gives 5 × 0.419 ≈ 2.10 expected heads.

The trading so far tells me little. One counterparty bought at 3.6 and another sold at 2.3, so the signals roughly cancel.

**Spread:** Settlement can only be a whole number, and the standard deviation of the remaining heads is about 1.1. Informed traders will hit me whenever the true count lands outside my quotes. I'm setting the bid just above 1 and the ask just below 3, roughly centred on 2.1. That captures most noise-trader flow while limiting losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 3.0}

Fair value is about 1.8 after the observed flip and trading. I'm quoting 0.9 / 2.9 so the settlement values next to fair value don't trade against me.

1. **Posterior on the coin after flip 1 = 0.** Weight each coin by its prior times P(tails):
   - p = 0.3: 0.2 × 0.7 = 0.14
   - p = 0.4: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18
   - p = 0.5: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25
   - Total is 0.57, so E[p] = (0.042 + 0.072 + 0.125) / 0.57 ≈ 0.42.

2. **Fair value.** With 5 flips left, expected heads are about 5 × 0.42 ≈ 2.1. The last counterparty sold to me at 1.2, which leans toward a low settlement. I shade fair value down to about 1.8.

3. **Bid at 0.9.** Settlement is a whole number of heads. An informed trader whose value is 1 sells only if my bid is above 1, so a bid of 0.9 avoids that trade. It still catches noise traders, whose valuation is about 1.8 ± 1.3. It also keeps my +1 long from growing cheaply against informed sellers.

4. **Ask at 2.9.** An informed trader buys only if the value is 3 or more. A noise trader buys about 20% of the time. Selling at 2.9 would also cut my long position.

{"bid": 0.9, "ask": 2.9}

The settlement value is now 0 or 1, because only flip 6 is still unknown.

**Fair value.** After five tails, I weight each coin by its prior times P(tails)^5:
- p = 0.3: 0.2 × 0.7^5 = 0.0336
- p = 0.4: 0.3 × 0.6^5 = 0.0233
- p = 0.5: 0.5 × 0.5^5 = 0.0156

Normalising these weights gives E[p] ≈ 0.375, so the fair value is 0.375.

**Informed traders.** Any ask at or above 1 and any bid at or below 0 can never be picked off by an informed trader, who knows the value is exactly 0 or 1. So I should only quote outside [0, 1].

**Ask.** Expected profit per quote is 0.5 × P(noise valuation > a) × (a − 0.375), with noise drawn from N(0.375, 1.3²):
- a = 1.0: about 0.099
- a = 1.3: about 0.11 (the best of the values tried)
- a = 1.5: about 0.109

**Bid.** By symmetry, a bid of about −0.5 gives an expected profit of roughly 0.11 from noise sellers.

{"bid": -0.5, "ask": 1.3}

Only flip 6 is still unknown, so the contract settles at either 0 or 1. Every revealed flip so far is tails.

**Updated coin probabilities after 5 tails**
- The weights (prior × chance of 5 tails) are: 0.2·0.7⁵ = 0.0336, 0.3·0.6⁵ = 0.0233, and 0.5·0.5⁵ = 0.0156.
- That makes the expected chance of heads about 0.375, so the fair value is about 0.375.

**Quoting bid 0 and ask 1**
- **Informed traders never trade.** If they know the value is 1, they won't buy at 1. If they know it is 0, they won't sell at 0. So they cannot pick me off.
- **Noise traders buy** when their valuation is above 1. This happens about 31% of the time and earns me about 0.625 per unit.
- **Noise traders sell** when their valuation is below 0. This happens about 39% of the time and earns me about 0.375 per unit.

Tightening either side would let informed traders trade against me. The extra noise-trader profit does not clearly cover that cost, so I keep 0 / 1. My position is +2, so buying one more unit stays within the limit.

{"bid": 36.4, "ask": 50.4}

- Fair coin: 0.4 × 0.5³ = 0.05
- Biased coin: 0.6 × 0.7³ = 0.2058

So the biased coin now has probability 0.2058 / 0.2558 ≈ 0.80. That makes the expected chance of heads on each remaining flip about 0.5 × 0.20 + 0.7 × 0.80 ≈ 0.66.

**Fair value.** The three heads already shown are worth 30. The four flips still to come are worth about 4 × 6.6 ≈ 26.4 more, so fair value is about 56.4. Someone also bought from me at 50.4 last stage, which nudges this up slightly, to roughly 56.5.

I'm short one contract, so I shift both prices up a little to make buying back more likely than selling more.

{"bid": 51.0, "ask": 63.0}

Three heads came up in flips 1–3. That pushes P(p=0.7) up to about 0.80, so the expected value is about 56.4 before looking at trades. The last counterparty sold to me at 51, which suggests a lower outcome is more likely. Weighting for that sale, I estimate fair value at about 52 and quote ±6 around it.

{"bid": 46.0, "ask": 58.0}

The contract settles at either 60 or 70, so I quote just outside that range. That way no informed trader will trade with me, and every noise trade has positive expected value.

**Which coin it is**

  - Fair coin: 0.4 × 0.5⁶ = 0.00625
  - Biased coin: 0.6 × 0.7⁶ ≈ 0.0706
- So P(coin is 0.7) ≈ 0.0706 / 0.0768 ≈ 0.919.

**Fair value**
- P(flip 7 is heads) ≈ 0.919 × 0.7 + 0.081 × 0.5 ≈ 0.684.
- Settlement is 60 if flip 7 is tails and 70 if heads.
- Fair value ≈ 60 + 6.84 = 66.84.

**Quote placement**
- **Bid 59.9:** an informed trader never sells below 60, so I only buy from noise traders.
  - A noise trader values below 59.9 with probability about 26%.
  - Each such buy is worth about 6.9 to me.
- **Ask 70.1:** an informed trader never buys above 70, so I only sell to noise traders.
  - A noise trader values above 70.1 with probability about 38%.
  - Each such sale is worth about 3.3 to me.
- A tighter ask such as 68 loses money. Informed traders would buy whenever flip 7 is heads, costing about 2 each time. That outweighs the extra noise-trader profit.
- My position is -2, so I have room to trade on either side.

{"bid": 59.9, "ask": 70.1}

Six heads out of six makes the 0.7 coin very likely (about 92%), so flip 7 is heads with probability about 0.68. The fair value is 60 + 6.8 ≈ 66.8, and settlement can only be 60 or 70.

- **Bid 59.9:** an informed trader never sells below 60, so only noise traders hit this bid. Each such fill gains about 6.9.
- **Ask 70.1:** an informed trader never buys above 70, so only noise traders lift this ask. Each such fill gains about 3.3.

Neither side can lose to an informed trader, so I'll keep the quote from the last step.
