- **Fair value:** flip 1 is already 0, and 5 flips remain, so fair value ≈ 5 × 0.473 ≈ 2.36.
- **Adjustment for trading:** the counterparty at quote 3 sold at my bid of 1.7. That hints the value may be a little lower, so I shade fair value to about 2.3.

I'm flat, so I quote roughly symmetrically around 2.3. The spread is wide enough to cover the risk of trading with an informed counterparty.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 3.0}

Fair value is about 0.81, so I'll quote a bid of 0.4 and an ask of 1.3.

**Which coin it is.** Four revealed flips are all tails.
- For the 0.4-heads coin: 0.6 × 0.6⁴ = 0.0778.
- For the 0.8-heads coin: 0.4 × 0.2⁴ = 0.00064.
- So P(the 0.8 coin) ≈ 0.008, and the chance of heads on each remaining flip is about 0.403.

**Fair value.** All revealed flips are 0, so settlement equals the heads in flips 5 and 6. The expected value is 2 × 0.403 ≈ 0.81.

**What an informed trader knows.** The settlement value can only be 0, 1 or 2:
- 0 with probability about 0.36.
- 1 with probability about 0.48.
- 2 with probability about 0.16.

**Choosing the spread.** Noise traders' valuations centre on 0.81 with standard deviation 1.6. A bid near 0.4 limits my loss to an informed seller holding a value of 0 to about 0.4. An ask near 1.3 limits my loss to an informed buyer holding a value of 2 to about 0.7. Both sides still capture noise flow. I am short 1, so I lean slightly toward buying.

{"bid": 0.4, "ask": 1.3}

Fair value is about 0.82. After four tails the coin is almost certainly the 0.4 coin (posterior about 99.2%), so the two remaining flips are worth about 2 × 0.403 ≈ 0.81. The informed buy at 1.3 last quote nudges this slightly higher.

The final count of heads from flips 5 and 6 is 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities of about 0.36, 0.48 and 0.16.

**Ask:** I priced each ask by what noise buyers pay me minus what informed buyers take from me.
- At 1.3, noise buyers earn me about +0.15, but informed buyers cost about 0.02 when the true count is 2.
- At 1.6, the net is about +0.18.
- At 2.0, noise buyers earn about +0.22. Informed buyers never lift it, since the count cannot exceed 2.
- At 2.2, the net is about +0.215, so the gain has levelled off.

I'll ask 2.0. Selling one more unit takes me to -3, which is allowed.

**Bid:** At 0, informed sellers never hit me, because the count cannot be below 0. Noise sellers still hit about 30% of the time, which is worth about +0.20.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 2.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 7/10, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value: the coin's expected heads probability is 0.7·0.5 + 0.3·0.7 = 0.56. Over 6 flips that gives 3.36 expected heads, so the contract is worth about 5 × 3.36 = 16.8.

Uncertainty: the variance in heads is about 1.78 (coin-flip noise plus uncertainty about which coin it is). That is a standard deviation of about 1.33 heads, or about 6.7 in contract value.

Settlement only takes multiples of 5 (…10, 15, 20, 25…), so informed traders cross my quotes at those levels. I set the bid below 15 and the ask above 20. Then informed traders only trade when the value is at least 5 away from fair value. Noise traders, whose valuations spread about 9.9 around fair value, still trade often enough to pay for the spread.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 22.0}

The contract is worth about 16.8 on public information, so I'm quoting around that.

- **Fair value:** the expected chance of heads is 0.7 × 0.5 + 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.56. Over 6 flips that gives 3.36 expected heads. At 5 per head, the expected settlement is 16.8.
- **Spread:** the settlement value is quite uncertain, with a standard deviation of roughly 6. Informed traders will pick off a tight quote, so I'm keeping the spread wide.
- **Change from last quote:** the 11.5 / 22 quote drew no trade, which hints the value is near the middle. I'm tightening slightly to 12.5 / 21.5 to catch more noise-trader flow.

{"bid": 12.5, "ask": 21.5}

Prior mean heads per flip = 0.56, so the expected number of heads is 3.36 and the prior fair value is 16.8.

A sell at 12.5 suggests a lower value. An informed seller implies a settlement value below 12.5, meaning 2 or fewer heads. That pulls the public fair value down a bit, to roughly 15.5–16.

The standard deviation of the settlement value is about 6. I'll quote around 15.5 with a spread wide enough to cover adverse selection. Since I'm long, I'll skew the quote slightly lower.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 19.5}

After flip 1 came up heads, the chance this is the biased coin (P(heads) = 0.7) rises from 0.3 to 0.375. Next-flip heads probability is then 0.625×0.5 + 0.375×0.7 = 0.575.

Expected heads = 1 + 5×0.575 = 3.875, so fair value ≈ 19.4. The stage 1 trades were one sell and one buy, so they roughly cancel and don't shift this estimate.

Five flips are still unknown, so the settlement value has a standard deviation of about 5.5. Informed traders will pick off a narrow quote, so I'll quote roughly ±4 around 19.4.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 23.5}

With flip 1 = heads, I estimate fair value at about 19.4. I quote roughly ±4–5 around it so that informed traders only trade at extreme outcomes.

**Updating on the coin.** Before any flips, the chance the coin is biased (0.7) is 0.3.
- After seeing heads: P(biased) = (0.3 × 0.7) / (0.3 × 0.7 + 0.7 × 0.5) = 0.21 / 0.56 = 0.375.
- So the expected heads probability for future flips is 0.5 + 0.2 × 0.375 = 0.575.

**Fair value.**
- Five flips remain, so expected further heads = 5 × 0.575 = 2.875.
- Total expected heads = 1 + 2.875 = 3.875, so fair value ≈ 5 × 3.875 = 19.4.
- The trades in stage 1 roughly cancel out, and the lack of a trade at quote 4 adds little information.

**Uncertainty and quote placement.** The settlement standard deviation is about 5 × √(5 × 0.25) ≈ 5.6.
- With a bid of 15, an informed trader sells only if settlement is 15 or less (3 or fewer total heads).
- With an ask of 24, an informed trader buys only if settlement is 25 or more (5 or more total heads).
- Noise traders (spread 9.9 around fair value) will still trade fairly often at these prices.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 24}

Posterior after flip1=1: P(0.7) = 0.3·0.7/(0.3·0.7+0.7·0.5)=0.21/0.56=0.375. Expected p for remaining = 0.375·0.7+0.625·0.5=0.575. Value = 5·(1+5·0.575)=5·3.875=19.4. Past no-trades with quotes around 15–24 are mildly informative but symmetric-ish. Settlement range: 5 remaining flips, sd of heads ~1.1 → value sd ~5.5+. Informed trades are where risk lies; quote around ±4.5.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 24}

**Fair value.** Two heads and two tails have been seen.
- Likelihood under the fair coin: 0.5⁴ = 0.0625.
- Likelihood under the biased coin: 0.7² × 0.3² = 0.0441.
- With priors of 0.7 and 0.3, the probability the coin is biased is 0.0132 / 0.0570 ≈ 0.23.
- So P(heads) ≈ 0.5 + 0.2 × 0.23 ≈ 0.546.
- Flips 5 and 6 are expected to give 1.09 heads, so fair value ≈ 5 × 3.09 ≈ 15.5.

**Possible settlements.** Only flips 5 and 6 are unknown, so the contract settles at 10, 15 or 20.
- Settles at 10 with probability ≈ 0.21.
- Settles at 15 with probability ≈ 0.48.
- Settles at 20 with probability ≈ 0.31.

**Where to quote.** I estimated expected profit per quote for each side.
- **Bid below 10:** informed traders never sell to me. Noise traders (centred on 15.5, sd 9.9) still sell sometimes, and I gain about 7.5 each time. Expected profit is about 0.84 at a bid of 8, against about 0.62 at a bid of 11.
- **Ask above 20:** informed traders never buy from me. Expected profit from noise traders is about 0.84 at an ask of 23, against about 0.74 at 20.1.

So I quote 8 / 23. Informed traders never trade with me there, and I collect the widest edge from noise traders.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 23}

Fair value is about 15.5, and the only settlement values still possible are 10, 15 and 20.

**Coin bias.** Two heads in four flips favours the fair coin.
- Weight for the fair coin: 0.7 × 0.5⁴ ≈ 0.0438.
- Weight for the 0.7 coin: 0.3 × 0.7² × 0.3² ≈ 0.0132.
- So P(biased coin) ≈ 0.23.
- That gives P(heads) for the two remaining flips of about 0.5 + 0.2 × 0.23 ≈ 0.546.

**Settlement value.**
- Expected total heads ≈ 2 + 2 × 0.546 ≈ 3.09, so fair value ≈ 15.5.
- The maximum is 4 heads, so the last buy at 23 must have come from a noise trader.

**Quote choice.** I quote just outside the range of possible values.
- With a bid of 9.9 and an ask of 20.1, an informed trader never trades with me.
- A noise trader (fair value ±9.9) still hits either side about 16% of the time, at roughly 4.6–5.6 of edge.
- Tightening the ask to 15.1 would be worse. An informed trader who knows the value is 20 would buy there, a loss of about 0.73 per quote on average. The extra noise trades near fair value would earn only about 0.36 per quote.

{"bid": 9.9, "ask": 20.1}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 11 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 11. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
Fair value is 55. The number of red balls is uniform on 0 to 11, so the settlement is uniform on {0, 10, …, 110}.

I compared the expected profit of different asks. Each ask earns from noise traders (fair value plus Normal noise, sd 35) and loses to informed traders, who buy only when the true value is above the ask.

| Ask | Loss to informed | Gain from noise | Net per quote |
|-----|------------------|-----------------|---------------|
| 75  | 3.33             | 2.84            | −0.49         |
| 85  | 1.88             | 2.94            | +1.07         |
| 95  | 0.83             | 2.54            | +1.71         |
| 100 | 0.42             | 2.22            | +1.80         |
| 105 | 0.21             | 1.91            | +1.70         |

The best ask is about 100, which is 45 above fair value. The setup is symmetric, so the bid goes 45 below fair value, at 10.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 100}

No trade at 10/100 tells us little, so fair value stays near the prior mean of 55. I quote wide around it to limit losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 28, "ask": 82}

Two blue draws make red-poor urns more likely. Updating on that gives an expected 2.25 red balls, so the fair value is about 22.5.

**How I got 2.25:**
- The weight for each red count r is (11−r)(10−r), the chance both draws are blue.
- For r = 0 to 9 the weights are 110, 90, 72, 56, 42, 30, 20, 12, 6, 2, which sum to 440.
- Multiplying each weight by r gives 990.
- So the expected red count is 990 / 440 = 2.25.

**Why the spread is wide:**
- Half the counterparties know the true value, which still ranges roughly 0 to 90.
- The posterior is skewed upward: the true value could easily be 50 or more.
- So I set the ask further from fair value than the bid to limit losses to informed buyers.

Noise traders, whose valuation has standard deviation 35, will still trade often enough at these prices to make the quote worthwhile.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 38}

Fair value is about 22.5 after two blue draws. I'm quoting a bid of 10 and an ask of 47.

**Fair value.** Seeing two blue balls makes low red counts more likely: the posterior on R red balls is proportional to (11−R)(10−R).
- That gives P(R=0) = 0.25 and E[R] = 990/440 = 2.25.
- So the fair value is 10 × 2.25 = 22.5.
- The distribution is skewed right: about 16% chance that R ≥ 5, which means a value of 50 or more.

**Bid.** I compared the expected loss to informed sellers with the expected gain from noise sellers.
- At a bid of 10, informed traders sell only when R = 0 (a loss of 10 each time). Noise traders sell about 36% of the time, and I gain about 12.5 on each.
- That nets about +1.0 per quote. A bid of 12 nets only about +0.5, so 10 is better.

**Ask.** The same comparison favours a wide ask because of the long right tail.
- At an ask of 47, informed traders buy only when R ≥ 5, which happens about 16% of the time.
- Noise traders buy about 24% of the time, and I gain about 24.5 on each.
- That nets roughly +2.9 per quote, close to the best I found. An ask of 38 nets only about +0.7.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 47}

Three blue draws in a row push the estimate down to about 16, so I'm quoting a 5 bid and a 27 ask around that.

**Fair value.** The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform over 0 to 11. After three blue draws, the weight on each R is proportional to (11−R)(10−R)(9−R). That gives R = 0 about 33% probability and R = 1 about 24%, with the weights falling off steeply after that. The posterior mean of R is about 1.6, so the expected settlement is about 16.

**Bid at 5.**
- An informed seller only hits the bid when the true value is 0. That has about a 33% chance and costs me 5 each time.
- A noise trader sells below 5 about 38% of the time, and I gain about 11 per unit.
- The bid is roughly break-even to slightly positive.

**Ask at 27.**
- An informed buyer lifts the offer when the true value is 30 or more. That has about a 25% chance.
- When it happens, I lose about 14 per unit, because the average value in those cases is near 41.
- A noise trader buys above 27 about 38% of the time, and I gain about 11 per unit.
- The ask is roughly break-even too, so it is acceptable.

I'm short 1 unit, so a fill on the bid would also flatten my position.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 27}

The public fair value is about 16, so I'm quoting a bid of 4 and an ask of 28, leaning slightly up because I'm short.

**Fair value from the draws.** The prior is uniform over 0–11 red balls. The chance of drawing 3 blues in a row is proportional to (11−R)(10−R)(9−R). That makes the posterior chance of each red count proportional to:

| Red balls | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 990 | 720 | 504 | 336 | 210 | 120 | 60 | 24 | 6 |

- The weights sum to 2970.
- The expected number of red balls is 4752 / 2970 = 1.6.
- So the expected settlement value is about 16.

**Trading history.** The two buys at my ask (47 and 27) push this up slightly. They could have come from informed traders, but they are also plausible as noise trades.

**Bid.** At 4, an informed trader would only sell if the value is 0, so my loss would be small. Noise traders selling below 4 are profitable for me.

**Ask.** I'm at −2, so I can sell one more unit. At 28 I'm well above fair value, and an informed trader buys only if the value is 30 or more, which has low probability.

{"bid": 4, "ask": 28}

With four blue draws, the expected settlement value is about 11.67. Any bid above 0 loses money to informed sellers when the urn holds 0 red balls. A negative bid still earns from noise traders, and expected profit is highest around a bid of -10 to -15.

**Posterior.** The chance of drawing 4 blue balls given R red balls is proportional to C(11−R, 4). For R = 0 to 7 the weights are 330, 210, 126, 70, 35, 15, 5, 1, which sum to 792.

- Expected red balls: E[R] = 924/792 ≈ 1.167, so the fair value is about 11.67.
- Probabilities: V=0 is 0.417, V=10 is 0.265, V=20 is 0.159, V=30 is 0.088, and higher values share the rest.

**Expected profit by bid.** An informed trader sells only if the value is strictly below my bid. A noise trader sells if 11.67 plus Normal(0, 35) noise is below my bid.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 5 | ≈ +0.37 |
| 0 | ≈ +2.16 |
| -10 | ≈ +2.90 |
| -15 | ≈ +2.99 |
| -20 | ≈ +2.90 |

The curve is flat around -10 to -15, so I'll bid -12.

{"bid": -12, "ask": null}

Posterior fair value is about 11.67 (after four blue draws, E[red] = 924/792 ≈ 1.17 balls).

- **Bids at 0 or below:** informed sellers never hit the bid. The only possible true values are multiples of 10 (0, 10, 20, …), and an informed counterparty only sells if its value is strictly below my bid.
- **Bids above 0:** an informed counterparty with value 0 would sell to me, and that costs money.
- **Noise traders:** they sell when their valuation (about 11.67 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 35) falls below my bid. I gain the gap between 11.67 and my bid on each such trade.

Expected profit from noise sellers alone, for a few bids:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 0 | ≈ 2.16 |
| -5 | ≈ 2.64 |
| -10 | ≈ 2.90 |
| -15 | ≈ 2.97 |
| -20 | ≈ 2.90 |

The best bid is around -15. My position is -3, so the ask side is pulled and I quote the bid only.

{"bid": -15, "ask": null}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 5 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The fair value before any reveal is 17.5. I'll quote about 4.5 either side of it.

**Fair value**
- The expected chance of heads averages the three coin types: 0.2·0.2 + 0.3·0.7 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.04 + 0.21 + 0.45 = 0.70.
- Expected heads over 5 flips is 5 × 0.70 = 3.5.
- The contract pays 5 per head, so the expected settlement is 5 × 3.5 = 17.5.

**Spread**
- The settlement value can land anywhere from 0 to 25, so it is quite uncertain.
- One trader in five is informed and knows the exact value. A wide spread limits what they can take from me.
- Noise traders' valuations vary by 12 around fair value, so a spread of about ±4.5 still lets many of them trade with me.

{"bid": 13.0, "ask": 22.0}

The coin's prior heads probability averages 0.7, so before any trading the expected settlement was 5 × 5 × 0.7 = 17.5.

**What the first trade tells us**
- The only settlement above 22 is 25 (all five flips heads). Its prior probability is about 0.3455.
- **If the value is 25:** a buy at 22 happens with probability about 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.354 ≈ 0.483. An informed counterparty always buys, and a noise trader buys about 35% of the time.
- **Otherwise:** a buy happens with probability about 0.8 × 0.354 ≈ 0.283, from noise traders only.

**Updated value**
- Given the value is not 25, its expected value is about 13.5.
- Weighting the two cases by these likelihoods gives a fair value of about 19.

**Quote**
I'm short one unit, so I lean slightly toward buying and center the quote around 18.5–19. I keep the spread wide to guard against informed traders.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 23.5}

Flip 1 came up heads, so I updated the odds for each coin with Bayes' rule:

| P(heads) | Prior | × chance of heads | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.04 | 0.057 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | 0.21 | 0.300 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.45 | 0.643 |

Total weight for heads is 0.70, so the expected P(heads) for the next flip is 0.56 / 0.70 = 0.8.

Settlement is 5 × (1 known head + 4 remaining flips × 0.8) = 5 × 4.2 = **21**.

The trading history nudges this up a little. Someone bought at 22 and nobody traded at 14 / 23.5, so I put fair value at about 21.3.

I'm short 1, so I shift both prices slightly upward. I keep the spread wide enough to protect against informed traders.

{"bid": 17, "ask": 25.5}

Fair value is about 21, so I'm quoting 16.5 bid and 25 ask around it.

1. **Coin after flip 1 = heads.** Each prior is multiplied by that coin's chance of heads:
   - 0.2 coin: 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04
   - 0.7 coin: 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.21
   - 0.9 coin: 0.5 × 0.9 = 0.45

   These total 0.70, so the updated chances are about 0.057, 0.300 and 0.643.

2. **Chance of heads on each remaining flip:** 0.057 × 0.2 + 0.3 × 0.7 + 0.643 × 0.9 ≈ 0.80.

3. **Fair value:** expected heads = 1 + 4 × 0.80 = 4.2, so the expected settlement is 5 × 4.2 = 21. I'm treating the trading history as only a small adjustment.

4. **Quote:** settlement can still land anywhere from 5 to 25, so an informed trader can hurt me a lot and I keep the spread wide. I'm short 1, so I keep the ask at the highest possible settlement (25) to avoid getting shorter. I bring the bid a little closer to fair value to invite a buy that reduces the short.

{"bid": 16.5, "ask": 25}

Fair value: after two heads the posterior coin bias is about P(heads) ≈ 0.84. The expected settlement is 5 × (2 + 3 × 0.8375) ≈ 22.6.

- **Ask 25:** The settlement can't exceed 25, so an ask there never loses to an informed buyer. Noise traders still buy fairly often, at roughly 42%.
- **Bid 19:** This sits below fair value. An informed seller only hits it when the settlement is 15 or 10.

{"bid": 19, "ask": 25}

After two heads, the coin is most likely one of the high-bias coins.

**Posterior on the coin after flips 1 and 2 are both heads**

| P(heads) | Prior | P(HH) | Prior × P(HH) | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.04 | 0.008 | 0.014 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | 0.49 | 0.147 | 0.263 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.81 | 0.405 | 0.723 |

The products sum to 0.56. Weighting each P(heads) by its posterior gives an expected P(heads) of about 0.8375.

**Fair value**
- Two heads are already known and three flips remain.
- Fair value = 5 × (2 + 3 × 0.8375) ≈ 22.6.
- Quote 5's sale at 19 hints slightly lower, but one trade is weak evidence, so I mostly ignore it.

**Ask**
- Settlement can only be 10, 15, 20 or 25, so an informed trader never values the contract above 25.
- An ask of 25.1 can therefore only be lifted by noise traders, at a profit of about 2.5 per trade.

**Bid**
- A bid of 19 is about 3.6 below fair value, which cushions against selling by informed traders.
- I am flat, so I can quote both sides with no inventory skew.

{"bid": 19, "ask": 25.1}

With four heads revealed, the fair value is about 24.3. The contract can only settle at 20 or 25, so quoting at those two prices means an informed trader never trades against me.

**Posterior on the coin after 4 heads:**

| P(heads) | Prior | × likelihood (p⁴) | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 | × 0.0016 | 0.00032 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | × 0.2401 | 0.0720 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | × 0.6561 | 0.3281 |

The weights sum to 0.4004.

**Fair value:**
- P(flip 5 is heads) = (0.2·0.00032 + 0.7·0.0720 + 0.9·0.3281) / 0.4004 ≈ 0.864.
- Fair value = 20 + 5 × 0.864 ≈ 24.3.

**Why 20 and 25:**
- The settlement is either 20 or 25.
- At an ask of 25, an informed trader who knows the value is 25 will not buy, because the value is not above the ask.
- At a bid of 20, an informed trader who knows the value is 20 will not sell.
- Noise traders still trade at these prices. Their valuations spread about 12 points around 24.3, so many fall below 20 or above 25.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 25}

Fair value is about 24.3, so I'm quoting a bid of 15 and an ask of 33.

1. **Which coin it is.** Four heads in a row make the coin very likely the 0.9 one.
   - P(4 heads | coin) is 0.0016 for the 0.2 coin, 0.2401 for the 0.7 coin and 0.6561 for the 0.9 coin.
   - Weighting by the priors gives posteriors of about 0.1%, 18.0% and 81.9%.

2. **Fair value.** P(flip 5 is heads) = 0.001×0.2 + 0.180×0.7 + 0.819×0.9 ≈ 0.864. Settlement is 25 with that probability and 20 otherwise, so fair value ≈ 20 + 5×0.864 ≈ 24.32.

3. **Informed traders.** Settlement can only be 20 or 25. With an ask of at least 25 and a bid of at most 20, an informed trader never trades with me. So only noise traders matter.

4. **Best quotes against noise traders.** A noise trader's valuation is roughly Normal with mean 24.32 and standard deviation 12. I want the price that maximises (edge over fair value) × (chance they trade).
   - **Ask:** 32 gives about 7.68 × 0.26 ≈ 2.0, and 34 gives about 9.68 × 0.21 ≈ 2.0. The best ask is around 33.
   - **Bid:** 16 gives about 8.32 × 0.24 ≈ 2.0, and 14 gives about 10.32 × 0.20 ≈ 2.0. The best bid is around 15.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 33}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
With a uniform prior on 0–10 red balls, the fair value is 5. I quote wide because 35% of counterparties know the true count.

I compared spreads by expected profit per side: the gain from noise traders crossing my price minus the loss to informed traders.
- **±2.5 (2.5 / 7.5):** about +0.10 per side.
- **±3 (2 / 8):** about +0.12 per side, the best of those I checked.
- **±3.5 (1.5 / 8.5):** about +0.10 per side.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

The fair value is about 2.9, so I'll quote a bid of 1.6 and an ask of 4.2, roughly 1.3 either side.

**Prior after draw 1 = blue.** The chance of drawing blue first is (10−R)/10, so the posterior weight on R red balls is proportional to (10−R). That gives a mean of 165/55 = 3.0.

**Effect of the two trades.** I scored each possible R by how likely the observed trades were under it:
- **Buy at 8:** An informed trader buys only if R ≥ 9. A noise trader centred near 5 with standard deviation 2.4 buys with probability about 0.106. So this trade's likelihood is about 0.35·[R≥9] + 0.069.
- **Sell at 5.6:** I assumed the public fair value was about 5.5 at that point. A noise trader then sells with probability about 0.5, and an informed trader sells if R ≤ 5. So this trade's likelihood is about 0.33 + 0.35·[R≤5].

**Posterior.** Multiplying (10−R) by both likelihoods:

| R | Weight |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.469 |
| 1 | 0.422 |
| 2 | 0.375 |
| 3 | 0.328 |

- **Informed traders:** they only sell when the true count is 4 or fewer, which has about 17% probability. The average loss on those trades is about 1.4, costing roughly 0.08 per quote.

The ask side is symmetric, so the tighter quote has positive expected value on both sides.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 7.1}

At quote 2 someone sold to me at 4.9. That leans slightly bearish, because an informed trader sells only when the true count is 4 or less. That pulls my fair value down to about 5.2.

I'm already long 1, so I skew my quotes a little lower around 5.2. The spread is fairly wide to protect against informed traders.

The draws give a fair value of about 5.6. Since I am already long 2, I set the quotes around 5.2–5.3 and skew them down to shed inventory.

**Fair value from the draws.** One blue and one red have been drawn. The 8 balls left in the urn are each red with probability 0.6, so their red count follows Binomial(8, 0.6).
- Mean of the remaining reds: 8 × 0.6 = 4.8.
- Expected settlement: 1 (the red already drawn) + 4.8 = 5.8.
- Standard deviation: √(8 × 0.6 × 0.4) ≈ 1.39.

**What the trade history says.** Counterparties sold to me twice, at 4.9 and at 4. An informed seller at 4 would mean the value is 3 or less, which needs at most 2 reds among the remaining 8. That is unlikely, so those sells were probably mostly noise. They still pull the estimate down a little, to about 5.6.

**Quote placement.** I lean lower than 5.6 because of my position. The spread is wide enough to limit losses to informed traders on both sides:
- At an ask of 6.2, an informed trader buys only when the value is 7 or more.
- At a bid of 4.2, an informed trader sells only when the value is 4 or less.

{"bid": 4.2, "ask": 6.2}

With one red and one blue drawn, the other 8 balls are each red with probability 0.6. So the expected count is 1 + 8 × 0.6 = **5.8**.

The last trade was a buy at my ask of 6.2. An informed buyer there would mean the true count is 7 or more. I raise my estimate slightly to about **6.0**.

On spread, the noise traders have a standard deviation of 2.3 and 35% of counterparties are informed. A half-spread of about 1.2 balances the gain from noise traders against losses to informed ones.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 11 balls, each red or blue. Each ball was independently painted red with probability 0.3. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
The prior fair value is 33, because 11 balls × 0.3 × 10 = 33. The value's standard deviation is about 15, since √(11 × 0.21) ≈ 1.52 balls, times 10. Informed traders make up 35% of counterparties, so I'm setting a fairly wide spread of about ±8 around 33 to protect against them.

{"bid": 25, "ask": 41}

Fair value 33, sd of settlement 10*sqrt(11*0.21)=15.2. No trade last time is slightly informative but fair stays ~33. Keep similar spread, slightly tighter.

{"bid": 26, "ask": 40}

Fair value 33. Settlement SD = 10*sqrt(11*0.21)=15.2. No trades so far implies little info. Quote around 33 with spread ~±7.

{"bid": 26, "ask": 40}

Since each ball's colour is independent, the two balls we have seen are known exactly: one red, one blue. The other 9 balls are still red with probability 0.3 each.

- Expected red balls = 1 + 9 × 0.3 = 3.7.
- Fair value = 10 × 3.7 = 37.
- Standard deviation of the value = 10 × √(9 × 0.21) ≈ 13.7.

An informed counterparty knows the true value, so I quote a wide spread around 37 to limit losses to them. I'll post a bid of 30 and an ask of 44.

{"bid": 30, "ask": 44}

Draws so far show 1 red and 1 blue. The other 9 balls are each red with probability 0.3, so before the trade the expected value was 10 × (1 + 2.7) = 37.

**Update on the sell at 30.** A seller at 30 is either informed or noise.
- **Informed seller:** this only happens if the true value is 20 or less, meaning at most 1 more red ball. That has probability about 0.196. So this case has weight 0.35 × 0.196 ≈ 0.069, and its conditional mean value is about 17.9.
- **Noise seller:** their valuation falls below 30 with probability about 0.26. So this case has weight 0.65 × 0.26 ≈ 0.170, and its value is still around 37.
- **Posterior fair value:** (0.069 × 17.9 + 0.170 × 37) / 0.239 ≈ 31.5.

**Quote.** I centre near 31 and keep the spread wide, because informed traders are 35% of arrivals. I shade slightly lower because I am already long 1.

{"bid": 24, "ask": 38}

Since the balls were painted independently, each of the 9 undrawn balls is red with probability 0.3. After draw 1 = red and draw 2 = blue, the expected count is 1 + 0.3 × 9 = 3.7 red balls, so the base value is 37.

Trading history shifts this a little. At quote 4 someone sold to me at 30, which hints the value is low. At quote 5 no one traded inside 24–38, which is mildly neutral. Treating the quote-4 sale as weak evidence puts fair value near 35.

I am long one unit, so I shade my quotes slightly lower to make selling more likely than buying. That gives a bid of 28 and an ask of 41.

{"bid": 28, "ask": 41}

Known so far: 2 red among the 3 revealed draws. The other 8 balls are each red independently with probability 0.3, so the expected number of red among them is 8 × 0.3 = 2.4.

- Expected total red = 2 + 2.4 = 4.4, so public fair value = 44.
- Standard deviation of settlement: 10 × √(8 × 0.3 × 0.7) ≈ 13.

Trade history also carries some information. At quote 4, a counterparty sold to us at 30 when public fair value was 10 × (1 + 9 × 0.3) = 37. That sale hints slightly that the value is lower. Still, the public fair value is defined from the reveals, so I take 44.

On spread: an informed trader moves the expected value by roughly ±10 or more given the 13 standard deviation. Set against the 11 standard deviation of noise traders, a half-spread of about 7 seems reasonable.

I am long 1, so I skew the quotes down slightly to lean toward selling.

{"bid": 36, "ask": 50}

Each ball is painted independently, so the 8 undrawn balls are still each red with probability 0.3. That gives an expected 2.4 red among them.

Revealed red balls so far: 2 (draws 1 and 3).

Expected value = 10 × (2 + 2.4) = 44.

The trade history adds a little information: one sale at 30 and several no-trades. That is only weak evidence, so I keep fair value near 44.

The settlement value has standard deviation 10 × √(8 × 0.3 × 0.7) ≈ 13. An informed trader's valuation therefore often sits far from fair value, and the spread should be fairly wide. I am long 1 unit, so I shade the quotes slightly lower to make selling a bit more likely than buying.

{"bid": 37, "ask": 50}

Three of the four draws were red, so at least 3 of the 11 balls are red. The other 7 balls were each painted red independently with probability 0.3, so the draws tell us nothing more about them. That gives an expected value of 10 × (3 + 7 × 0.3) = 51.

The counterparties sold to me at 37 and 35 during stage 3. That nudges the estimate slightly toward the lowest outcome of 30, so I put public fair value around 49–50.

I'm at +3, so only the ask is allowed, and I'm happy to sell. Setting the ask a little above fair value at 53 means I usually sell to noise traders at a gain. It also limits how much the informed counterparty takes when the value is 60 or more.

{"bid": null, "ask": 53}

Given 3 red balls among the 4 drawn, each of the other 7 balls is still red with probability 0.3. That gives an expected red count of 3 + 7 × 0.3 = 5.1, so the fair value is 51. The settlement value can only be 30, 40, 50, 60 and so on, with roughly 23% weight on 60, 10% on 70 and 3% on 80 or more.

I'm long 3, so only the ask is open. Selling below 60 loses to informed traders whenever the value is 60 or more. An ask just above 60 means informed traders only buy at 70 or more. Noise traders with valuation 51 + N(0, 11) still lift it about 18% of the time.

Expected profit by ask, after informed losses:
- 55: about −0.24
- 59.9: about +0.64
- 61: about +0.67
- 65: about +0.59

So I'll post an ask of 61.

{"bid": null, "ask": 61}

Pick the ask that maximises expected profit on one possible sale.

**Fair value.** Three of the four drawn balls were red. Each of the 7 balls left in the urn is still red with probability 0.3, independently. So the expected red count is 3 + 7 × 0.3 = 5.1, and fair value is 51. The two asks I posted at 53 and 61 in stage 4 did not trade, which fits a public fair value near 51.

**Settlement distribution.** Settlement is 30 plus 10 times the number of red balls among the 7 still in the urn:

| Remaining reds | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 60 | 0.227 |
| 4 | 70 | 0.097 |
| 5 | 80 | 0.025 |
| 6 | 90 | 0.004 |

**Expected profit by ask level.**
- Noise traders (probability 0.65) value the contract at 51 plus noise with standard deviation 11. A sale to them earns ask − 51 on average.
- An informed trader (probability 0.35) buys only when settlement is above the ask, so every sale to them loses money.

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 55 | +0.93 | −1.17 | −0.24 |
| 61 | +1.18 | −0.51 | +0.67 |
| 62 | +1.14 | −0.47 | +0.67 |
| 65 | +0.93 | −0.34 | +0.59 |
| 69.9 | +0.54 | small | about +0.40 |

The best range is 61 to 62, so I quote an ask of 61.5. The bid stays null because I am at +3 and cannot buy.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 8 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 8. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
Fair value is 40: the number of red balls is uniform on 0 to 8, so the expected settlement is 10 × 4. Half the counterparties know the true value, and the value can be anywhere from 0 to 80. That means a tight quote loses more to informed traders than it earns from noise traders.

Expected profit per quote on the ask side at 40 + d (the bid side is symmetric):
- At d = 15, I expect to lose about 0.9.
- At d = 25, I expect to gain about 0.07.
- At d = 30, I expect to gain about 0.3. This is close to the best; d = 35 gives about the same.

So I quote 30 either side of fair.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 70}

Fair value is 40, since the number of red balls is uniform on 0–8 and the contract pays 10 per red ball. I compared a few symmetric quotes around 40, looking only at the ask side; the bid side is symmetric.

| Ask | Expected loss to informed buyers | Expected gain from noise buyers | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 55 | Value 60, 70 or 80 (prob 3/9), avg loss 15 → 0.5 × 3/9 × 15 ≈ 2.5 | P(noise > 55) ≈ 0.215, gain 15 → 0.5 × 0.215 × 15 ≈ 1.6 | Negative |
| 60 | Value 70 or 80 (prob 2/9), avg loss 15 → 0.5 × 2/9 × 15 ≈ 1.67 | P(noise > 60) ≈ 0.146, gain 20 → 0.5 × 0.146 × 20 ≈ 1.46 | About even |
| 65 | Value 70 or 80 (prob 2/9), avg loss 10 → 0.5 × 2/9 × 10 ≈ 1.11 | P(noise > 65) ≈ 0.094, gain 25 → 0.5 × 0.094 × 25 ≈ 1.17 | Slightly positive |

A spread of 15/65 is the only one of these with a slightly positive expected edge, so I'll quote that.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 65}

With nothing revealed and no trades yet, fair value is 40: the red-ball count is uniform on 0 to 8, so the expected settlement is 10 × 4.

**What the two no-trade quotes tell me.** An informed counterparty would have traded against 15 / 65 if the true value were 0, 10, 70 or 80. Since nobody did, an informed trader's value is now most likely one of 20, 30, 40, 50 or 60. Fair value stays at 40 by symmetry.

**Choosing the ask** (expected profit per quote, with half the counterparties informed and half noise traders with standard deviation 19):
- **Ask 45:** I lose to informed buyers at 50 and 60 more than I gain from noise buyers, about −1.
- **Ask 55:** an informed buyer at 60 costs a little, but noise buyers make up for it, about +1.1.
- **Ask 59:** about +1.41, the best of those checked.
- **Ask 60:** an informed buyer only trades if the value is above 60, which it no longer can be. I earn about +1.46 from noise buyers alone (14.6% chance they buy, 20 points of edge, half the time).

By symmetry the bid goes at 20.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 60}

The first draw being blue shifts the posterior toward fewer red balls. The probability of r red balls is proportional to (8−r), so the fair value is 10 × 84/36 ≈ 23.3.

**Bid side.** An informed seller sells only when the value is 0 or 10, and those outcomes are likely (8/36 and 7/36).
- Bids near fair value lose to informed sellers about as much as they earn from noise traders.
- A bid near 2 nearly removes the informed loss (value 0 is still a small loss) and still earns from noise sellers, giving the best expected profit.

**Ask side.** The upside tail is thin, so an informed buyer is costly when the ask is close.
- At an ask of 35, informed buyers cost more than noise buyers pay, so the expected profit is negative.
- At an ask of 45, noise buyers pay about 2.8 per arrival against an informed loss of about 1.9, which is positive.

{"bid": 2, "ask": 45}

Fair value now is about 23.3. After draw 1 came out blue, the chance of each red count r is proportional to (8 − r). The expected number of red balls is 84/36 ≈ 2.33, so the fair value is about 10 × 2.33 = 23.3.

The possible settlement values are widely spread and skewed, so I quote wide to guard against informed traders:

- **Bid 8:** an informed trader only sells here when the value is 0 (probability about 22%).
- **Ask 40:** an informed trader only buys here when the value is 50 or more (probability 6/36, about 17%).

Noise traders still cross both sides often enough to pay for those losses.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 40}

The first draw came up blue, so I update the fair value on that.

**Fair value.** Each red-ball count r is weighted by (8−r), so the weights run 8, 7, …, 0 and sum to 36. The expected number of red balls is Σr(8−r)/36 = 84/36 ≈ 2.33. That makes fair value about 23.3. No trades have happened yet, so the trading history doesn't move this.

Each side's expected profit per quote is the noise-trader gain minus the informed-trader loss, each weighted by 0.5.

**Bid side.**
- At a bid of 10, an informed trader sells only when the value is 0 (weight 8/36). The loss is about 0.5 × 80/36 ≈ 1.11.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 0.24, earning about 13.3 each time, which gives about 1.6.
- Net is about +0.5, better than bidding 12, which roughly breaks even.

**Ask side.**
- At an ask of 45, an informed trader buys when the value is 50, 60 or 70. The loss is about 0.5 × 70/36 ≈ 0.97.
- A noise trader buys with probability about 0.13, earning about 21.7 each time, which gives about 1.38.
- Net is about +0.4, better than asking 40.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 45}

With two blue draws revealed, the fair value of the contract is 15.

**Fair value.** The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform over 0 to 8. Seeing two blue draws makes each R more or less likely in proportion to (8−R)(7−R).

| Settlement value | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.333 | 0.25 | 0.179 | 0.119 | 0.071 | 0.036 | 0.012 |

The expected value of R is 1.5, so the public fair value is 15.

**Bid.** The settlement value can never be below 0. At a bid of 0, an informed trader never sells to me profitably. A noise trader sells about 21% of the time, which is when its noise is below −15. That earns about 1.6 per quote on average. Bids above 0 lose more to informed traders than they gain from noise traders. Bids below 0 earn slightly less.

**Ask.** The expected loss to informed traders is about 0.6 at an ask of 35 and 0.3 at an ask of 40. The expected gain from noise traders is about 1.46 at 35 and 1.18 at 40. Both give a net expected profit of about 0.86 to 0.88, so I'll ask 38, between them.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 38}

With both revealed draws blue, the expected settlement value is 15. It is very likely to be near zero and occasionally much higher. That skew sets my quote.

**Posterior on red balls.** The chance of two blues is proportional to (8−r)(7−r)/56.

| Red balls r | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7–8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 56 | 42 | 30 | 20 | 12 | 6 | 2 | 0 |
| Probability | 0.333 | 0.250 | 0.179 | 0.119 | 0.071 | 0.036 | 0.012 | 0 |

- The total weight is 168, so the expected number of red balls is 252/168 = 1.5.
- Fair value is therefore 15, and settlement can only be 0, 10, …, 60.

**Ask side.** Expected profit per quote is half the noise traders' gain minus half the informed traders' loss.

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25 | 3.0 | 2.98 | ~0 |
| 30 | 3.2 | 1.79 | ~0.71 |
| 35 | 2.92 | 1.19 | ~0.87 |
| 40 | 2.35 | 0.60 | ~0.87 |

The curve is flat between 35 and 40, so I use an ask of about 38.

**Bid side.** The value is 0 one-third of the time, so any positive bid loses to informed sellers in that case.

| Bid | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3.2 | 0.33 | ~1.4 |
| 3 | 3.2 | 1.0 | ~1.1 |
| 5 | 3.0 | 1.67 | ~0.67 |
| 9 | 2.26 | 3.0 | negative |

A bid of 1 earns the most.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 38}

With two blue draws revealed, my posterior on the number of red balls R is weighted by (8−R)(7−R). That gives a mean of R = 1.5, so the public fair value is 15. There is a 1/3 chance that R = 0, meaning the contract settles at 0.

For each candidate price I compare two effects:
- **Profit from noise traders:** their valuation is 15 plus noise with standard deviation 19, so they sometimes trade at prices far from fair value.
- **Loss to informed traders:** they only trade when the true value is on the wrong side of my price.

**Ask side:**

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 35 | about 0.80 |
| 38 to 40 | about 0.88 (the best range) |
| 45 | about 0.68 |

I'll set the ask at 39, in the middle of the best range.

**Bid side:** The main risk is that the value is 0, which happens with probability 1/3. A bid of 1 loses only 1 per trade to informed sellers in that case. Bids of 0 and 1 both give about 1.4 to 1.6 in expected profit. Bids above 2 do worse, because losses to informed traders grow quickly. I'll bid 1.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 39}
